Definition from research

Boethius, De Musica, and the Architectural Structure of Miss MacIntosh, My Darling

I. The Word Count That Matters

The word music, including musician and musical, appears over 1,100 times in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling. The phrase music of the spheres or its equivalent, the silent or unheard music that Mr. Spitzer composes, appears nine times. Dead appears over 1,600 times. Love appears thousands of times across the novel's second half. These are not incidental repetitions. In a novel written over eighteen years by a scholar who controlled every sentence, a word that appears 1,100 times is a structural element.

The philosophical framework that makes this repetition architecturally coherent is Boethius's De Institutione Musica, his sixth-century treatise on the nature of music. Boethius divided music into three categories: musica mundana, the music of the spheres, the mathematical harmony of the cosmos that is inaudible to human ears; musica humana, the internal music of the human body, the harmony between body and soul; and musica instrumentalis, the audible music produced by singers and instruments. He said all reality is musical. His drawings in De Musica appear striking and may be an inspiration for the organization of Young's novel.

That may be one of the most significant architectural observations in the entire project. Young may have taken visual inspiration from Boethius's diagrams. The three-part structure of musica mundana, musica humana, and musica instrumentalis maps onto the three registers in which music operates throughout Miss MacIntosh: the cosmic, the interior, and the absent.

II. Musica Mundana: The Music No One Hears

Mr. Spitzer is the novel's primary musical consciousness. He is described as a composer of silent music, music he has written in scraps and fragments all his life, music that no one has ever played. His compositions are intended for an audience of the dead. He wonders whether there is such a thing as a non-aural music, a non-visual language, a reality not dependent upon the ear or the eye.

This is musica mundana translated into the novel's register. Boethius's music of the spheres is mathematically real but inaudible to human ears. Mr. Spitzer's music is compositionally real but unperformed, unheard, written for instruments no merely mortal musician could play. The parallel is exact. Mr. Spitzer inhabits the same structural position in the novel that musica mundana holds in Boethius's system: the highest category, the one that orders everything else, the one that exists most fully precisely because it cannot be directly heard.

He had added to his last will and musical testament, that his musical rags had not covered him, for there was no great tailor, no tailor but that mad tailor stitching in a dream... if he had known what he was doing in the first place... perhaps he never would have done so, but would have allowed his music to write him.

The music writes the composer. The cosmos composes itself. Musica mundana is not created by anyone; it exists in the mathematical relationships of the celestial bodies. Mr. Spitzer's silent music exists in the same way: not as a score that could be performed but as the structure of his consciousness, the harmony that organizes his grief and his love and his endless meditation on the dead. He is not the composer. He is the conduit.

III. Musica Humana: The Body and Soul in Argument

Boethius's musica humana is the harmony, or disharmony, between body and soul. It is the internal music of the human being, the tuning or mistuning of the self's parts. In Miss MacIntosh, the relationship between body and soul is one of the most persistently examined questions in the novel. The word soul appears over 250 times. Body appears throughout in relation to soul, most often in states of division, conflict, or uncertain reunion.

“Two tenants wrangled in an empty house, that which was his body and his soul.” Mr. Spitzer's formulation is pure musica humana: the internal music of a self whose parts are not in harmony, whose body and soul are tenants in the same house arguing over possession. Every character in the novel has a version of this dissonance. Catherine's body lies horizontal in bed while her consciousness travels through opium dreams that are more real to her than the body's location. Miss MacIntosh's body is ordinary and practical and fully present; her secret, her baldness, her history, is a soul that does not match the body's performance of normalcy. Vera's body is on a bus traveling through Indiana; her consciousness is everywhere and nowhere simultaneously.

Musica humana as a structural principle explains why the novel can move so fluidly between exterior event and interior consciousness without those movements feeling like violations of realism. The novel is not a realistic novel that has been interrupted by a stream of consciousness. It is a novel organized around the idea that the interior music of each character is as real and as architecturally significant as anything they do or say. The body and the soul are both instruments in the same composition. The composition requires both.

IV. Musica Instrumentalis: The Sounds That Are and Are Not Heard

Musica instrumentalis is Boethius's category for audible music, the music produced by singers and instruments. In Miss MacIntosh this category is populated with instruments that appear throughout: flutes, pianos, banjo, clarinet, violin, trumpet, the alpenhorn that Cousin Hannah owns and that Mr. Spitzer steals after her death, the seven-stringed harp whose strings bear the music of soul and spirit and astral body.

But musica instrumentalis in the novel is almost always either silent or heard by the wrong ears. The stone deaf man at the end of the novel, whom Vera falls in love with, has never heard a traffic horn in his travels across America. His musical voice rolls through silence. He hears not with ears but with eyes and fingers. The last reference to music in the novel is Vera's statement about loving this stone deaf man: his musical voice rolling through silence as I heard him who could not hear me. Musica instrumentalis, the category of audible music, ends in silence. The sound reaches only the one who cannot hear it.

This is Boethius inverted, and the inversion is the novel's most serious argument about music. Boethius's three categories are arranged hierarchically: musica mundana is highest, musica instrumentalis is lowest. Young takes the lowest category and makes it the novel's final image: the musical voice that cannot be heard, the love that communicates across the impossibility of shared sound. Musica instrumentalis does not disappear into the higher categories. It persists, imperfect, audible to those who have no ears for it, real precisely because it cannot be contained by the hierarchy that was supposed to organize it.

V. The Diagrams and the Novel's Visual Architecture

The idea that Boethius's drawings in De Musica appear striking and may be an inspiration for the organization of Young's novel points toward a dimension of the architectural argument that cannot be fully developed without the diagrams themselves. Boethius's visual representations of musical proportion, of the mathematical relationships between the three categories of music, of the hierarchy from the cosmic to the human to the instrumental, are geometric as well as conceptual. They organize space as well as sound.

If Young took visual as well as conceptual inspiration from these diagrams, then the organization of the novel's chapters may follow a spatial as well as a temporal logic. The chapters are not arranged as episodes in a sequence; they are arranged as positions in a structure. Catherine's opium chapters, Mr. Spitzer's legal and musical meditations, Vera's bus journey and her memories, Cousin Hannah's suffrage and her secret love, Esther Longtree's perpetual pregnancy: these may be positions in a Boethian diagram, each occupying a specific place in the hierarchy of musica mundana, musica humana, and musica instrumentalis, each demonstrating a different relationship between the cosmic order and the individual consciousness that cannot quite hear it. This is the architectural argument that most requires return to the novel itself. The diagrams in De Musica need to be laid beside the chapter structure of Miss MacIntosh and the correspondence traced. That work is the next pass. What this chapter establishes is the framework: Boethius said all reality is musical, and Young built a novel that proves it, at 1,198 pages, by demonstrating all three categories of music in every register of the novel from the cosmic to the corporeal to the finally, beautifully, inaudible.

Movement Two: The Five Pillars in the Traditions

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Homer Capehorn · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Plato and Platonism · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Astronomy · Homer’s Epics · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · The History of Opium

Definition from research

The copyright page of Miss MacIntosh, My Darling lists Young's previous publications before the novel begins. Two are poetry collections: Prismatic Ground (1937) and Moderate Fable (1944). The novel was begun in 1947 and not finished until 1963. This means Young was building the novel's philosophical architecture for sixteen years while her two collections of poetry sat on the copyright page as its declared ancestors. Young herself said that all her writing reflected common themes, that she had been thinking and writing about these things since she was nine years old. The poetry is not a precursor to the novel. It is the same project in a compressed form, the five pillars in their most concentrated state, before the accumulation of 1,198 pages expanded them to their full structural weight. For a reader who cannot yet commit to the novel, the poems are the door. For a reader who has already entered the novel, the poems are the architectural drawings.

The plural self pillar is visible in the poems decades before Mr. Spitzer arrives. In "Elegy for the Body," Young writes: "Oh, she was plural; She multiplied; All sparrows fell / If once she died." The movement here is identical to the novel's "Every heart is the other heart. Every soul is the other soul. Every face is the other face. The individual is the one illusion." Both make the same claim: the individual is not singular, and the death or disappearance of one particular person carries within it the death of something universal. The difference is scale. The poem compresses the claim into eight syllables. The novel gives it Miss MacIntosh: "hers had been the face of every face, the heart of every heart," and then spends the entire remaining narrative in the grief produced by that fact. The poem contains the philosophical position. The novel inhabits it.

The grief as permanent weather pillar appears in its purest form in "Strange Prophecy": "Only by bees will be visited / The lonely portals of the dead. / They will come intent on trade / Of light within that house of shade... The skull's enigma, what it was, / Become a hive for honey bees." Young takes the image of the skull, the most conventional emblem of mortality, and fills it with bees, with the productive hum of living things conducting their ordinary labor inside the space that death has emptied. This is grief as permanent weather made architecturally visible: the skull does not stop. The bees move through it. Life conducts its business inside the house of the dead. The novel's equivalent is the honey being made in Miss MacIntosh's skull after her death: "They will make their honey in her skull. She's sleeping in the grass, and you can hear the dead birds singing." Young wrote the poem in 1937. She embedded the image in the novel twenty-six years later in exactly the same form, because the philosophical claim had not changed. Grief does not empty the house. It fills it with a different kind of life.

The witness pillar runs through "Dubious Ground," one of the most formally precise poems in Prismatic Ground: a sleepwalker who is "always aware" of his surroundings, moving "lightly, with the small sound / Of dew stopped in the air," perceived from outside as part of the environment rather than separate from it. The sleepwalker does not interpret what he witnesses. He moves through it with a heightened, intuitive attention that operates below the threshold of analytical consciousness. This is exactly the quality Young gives to Vera as narrator: a consciousness that attends to everything, judges nothing, and allows the full weight of what it perceives to accumulate without premature resolution. The poem establishes the perceptual method. The novel applies it across 1,198 pages of accumulated observation.

The illusion as primary pillar appears in "That Apple Was Mental," which Young includes in Moderate Fable: "that apple was mental, a constellation of ideas." The poem asks whether something real can be invisible, whether sound can be inaudible yet exist as harmonious music, whether the mental and the physical are as distinct as we pretend. The poem's answer, worked out in Young's characteristic associative accumulation, is that they are not: "we eat and drink ideas, we are clothed with them." The novel's mother Catherine is the full-scale embodiment of this claim. Her opium house is full of Platonists and cherubim and Pythagoras shedding golden feathers because the mind's constructions are as real as any physical fact, possibly more so, because they are more densely inhabited. The poem states the epistemological position in fourteen lines. The novel gives it a bedroom and forty years of accumulated visitors.

Recursive construction is the pillar most visible in the formal relationship between the poems and the novel itself. "A Crystal Principle," from Moderate Fable, describes a world where even "accident unknown / And least departure" from crystalline order generates meaning, where "pattern in anomalies" persists, where the "miscreant heart" and the "outlaw rose" are as essential to the design as the crystal's perfect planes. Young is describing her own compositional method: a structure that builds by accumulation, that incorporates its own deviations, that generates patterns from the interplay of order and departure. The novel builds by exactly this method. Each chapter's deviation from what came before is part of the structure. Mr. Spitzer's socks, darned and redarned until they are not the same socks, are a crystal principle: identity persisting through replacement, structure maintained through accumulated change.

The poems also offer the most compressed versions of the novel's major characters. "Lot's Wife" is Miss MacIntosh: the woman who insists on not looking back, for whom the backward glance is the fatal error, whose entire pedagogical project with Vera is to prevent exactly the turning that Lot's wife performed and was punished for. "He who lives in what has flown is less than salt, is less than stone," the poem concludes, and this is Miss MacIntosh's argument in miniature, the argument she makes every time she demands that Vera reckon with current facts rather than inherited dreams. "Biography," the chess game with Lucifer in which the player loses not because he is wicked but because he is "distracted by the poetic," is Mr. Spitzer: "an old ballade, a witch's name, / A wraith of smoke...but not the game." The poems are character studies written before the characters were named.

"The Departure" is Esther Longtree: "the lady thineed / Autumnally walks... The snail meanwhile / Drawn cold as she, / Traces her still / Wan Odyssey / Across the purple / Leaves in flood, / Beautiful / Of her heart's blood." The slow walk, the deformed movement, the beauty inseparable from blood and suffering, the odyssey that is not heroic but simply continuous. Young wrote this poem a decade before Esther Longtree existed as a character. The image arrived first. The character grew to fill it.

"Ballad-Loving Woman," one of the most formally direct poems in the collections, is the novel's description of its own method: "With singing words from long ago / She knew that life will stay." The novel is built from accumulated singing words from long ago, from Boethius and Bunyan and Homer and the Old Woman in the Shoe and the passenger pigeon Martha, all the inherited forms of human knowledge and grief and comedy that Young assembled into a single structure that is also a voice, also a woman, also a long journey by bus through a Middle West that is also everywhere. "Ballad-loving woman / Who lived until she died." That is what the novel is. That is what her poetry always was.

For a reader who begins with the poems, particularly the shorter, more formally contained poems of Prismatic Ground, each one is a door into the novel's architecture. "Sky of Grasses" gives you grief as permanent weather in twelve lines. "Strange Prophecy" gives you the witness pillar in eight. "Lot's Wife" gives you Miss MacIntosh's entire philosophical position in a single image. "Elegy for the Body" gives you the plural self. "A Crystal Principle" gives you recursive construction. Enter any of these doors and you are already inside the novel's five pillars. The novel is what happens when you refuse to leave.

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Buddhism · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Plato and Platonism · Spinoza

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Genesis · Napoleon and Wellington · Revelation and the Apocalypse · The Bible · The History of Opium

Definition from research

The first sentence Young gives us about God in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is not a prayer or a theological argument or a scene of worship. It is a statement of condition: "God is the loneliest of all, and there is perhaps no God but what we dreamed, and there is no train." Three clauses, and each one performs a different operation on the religious tradition Young inherited. The first extends Christian sympathy to God as a sufferer rather than a sovereign. The second places the entire theological enterprise inside the epistemological framework of illusion as primary. The third collapses the metaphysical into the mundane, the God-question and the train-question arriving in the same grammatical space with the same answer: perhaps neither exists except as the dream of the person asking. This is not atheism. It is something structurally more complex: a religious sensibility that has absorbed the full weight of the tradition and refused to either accept or dismiss it, choosing instead to hold it as a question the novel will spend 1,198 pages not resolving.

Young builds her religious architecture on four distinct registers, each one carried by a different character, each one doing different work inside the five pillars. The registers are: Miss MacIntosh's practical piety (the religion of the verifiable), the mother Catherine's agnostic mysticism (the religion of the interior), Mr. Spitzer's theological pluralism (the religion of accumulated names), and Mr. Bonebreaker's evangelical Christianity (the religion of salvation and judgment). None of these is the novel's position. All four together constitute the novel's argument about what religion is and what it is for.

Miss MacIntosh's piety is the most plainly rendered and the most philosophically interesting precisely because it contradicts itself without embarrassment. She is the woman who insists on truth to nature, rejects illusions and false prophets, refuses the consolations of an imaginary life, and teaches Vera the Pilgrim's Progress alongside the population of Kansas. Her faith is expressed as labor and endurance: "God had been her harness-maker, that He had hung her harness with tinkling bells so that it might always be known where she was, even when she was in the shadows." This is theology as practical ethics, God as the craftsman who makes the harness for the work that must be done, the bells not announcing divine presence but simply making the worker findable in the dark. She also holds, without apparent contradiction, that God "had not created everything," that "He had left many things uncreated," which is the most unsentimental theological statement in the novel: a God with limitations, a creation with gaps, a universe in which the uncreated is as real as the created and the worker's job is to keep working regardless. The witness pillar runs through her entire religious sensibility: she sees the world plainly, she names what she sees, and she refuses to dress the gaps in creation with illusions she cannot personally verify. "God pity God," she says when confronted with the baldness that is her secret, the bald head that will undo her entire performance of normality, and the inversion is theologically precise: the God who did not finish creation deserves the same compassionate attention she extends to any other being facing the consequences of its own insufficiency.

The mother Catherine represents the novel's most paradoxical religious figure: she is the agnostic who lives inside a world more densely populated with the sacred than any orthodox believer in the novel. "She was the agnostic, but the angels surrounded her in her opium paradise, their fleecy wings outspreading, shadowing her cheek, and the harpers harped, and the seas were turned to glass." Young is not being ironic here. The mother's agnosticism is genuine: she does not believe in God as a metaphysical proposition. But her interior world is constituted entirely by the imagery of revelation, by seraphim and cherubim and apocalyptic seas of glass, because the imagery of the Christian tradition, accumulated over centuries, has become the available vocabulary for interior experience at a certain scale of intensity. Her father had set a table for the wandering angel, a salt shaker and a crystal goblet and a plate of gold for whoever might arrive from Tarsus or some far place. She rejected his faith but kept his hospitality: her house is always full, its rooms assigned to Plato and Spinoza and Wellington and the ghost of Cheops, all equally welcome, none more real than another. The illusion as a primary pillar is what permits this: if illusion is the primary mode of experience, then the agnostic's interior world can be more theologically rich than the believer's, because it is not constrained by the requirement of doctrinal consistency. Every figure who arrives is equally invited and equally imaginary and equally present, which is its own kind of sacred.

Mr. Spitzer carries the novel's most formally elaborate religious architecture: the passage in which he catalogs the names of God runs for a full page without pausing, and it is worth attending to as architecture rather than decoration. "God was not God in Himself, Mr. Spitzer believed, but in these pitiful images of God, these images which were but phantoms fading on the air." Then the list: the True Vine, the Bread of Life, the Gate, the Door, the Wine, the Only-Begotten, the Anointed, the Word, the Restorer, the Resurrection, the Great Spirit, the Light of the World, the Man of Sorrows, the Old Man, the King of Glory, the King of Kings, the Prince of Peace, the Good Shepherd, the Narrow Way, the Rose, the Thorn, the Risen, Immanuel, the Word made Flesh, the Advocate, the Intercessor, the Dove. The King of Light opposed "by the necessary King of Darkness, for if there were no darkness, then there should be no conception of light." This is the plural self pillar operating at theological scale: God is not a single being with a stable identity but a being constituted by the accumulation of every name human longing has ever assigned to the divine, each name a particular, the God behind them all a universal that may or may not exist independently of the names. Young also has Mr. Spitzer extend the catalog beyond Christianity to "the third heaven, the seventh heaven, Valhalla, Nirvana, the happy hunting grounds," collapsing the boundary between traditions with the same gesture she uses to assign Plato and Spinoza to the same house: all of it is equally real, equally imagined, equally necessary.

Mr. Bonebreaker is the novel's only practicing evangelical, and Young gives him the most physically specific presentation of any religious figure in the novel. He is "sallow and tall and stoop-shouldered, a fisherman on the waters of this stormy life, casting his wide net," carrying his Bible and his Bible literature and his long black umbrella, raindrops falling from his beaked nose and chin. He finds Miss MacIntosh just after her mastectomy, weak and wandering, and tells her that "for whom the Lord loveth, the Lord chasteneth," and gathers the stray lamb to the fold. Young is not mocking him, exactly. She is showing how evangelical Christianity operates at its most effective: it arrives in the specific moment of maximum vulnerability, it names the suffering as spiritually meaningful, it offers community and certainty and a framework in which the wound becomes evidence of divine love rather than mere biological bad luck. Miss MacIntosh, who has refused every illusion, leans on Bonebreaker's arm in the rain because the wound has undone her ordinary resistance and what he is offering is warmth in a cold district, which is what religion has always offered and what Young never dismisses as simply false.

The preacher who collapses the wedding rite and the burial rite in a single ceremony without anyone present noticing until it is too late is the novel's most condensed theological statement. He moves from "to love, honor, and obey, forsaking all others" to "Man that is born of woman...hath but a short time to live" to "earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust, brother to brother, deep calling to deep" without the flicker of an eyelid, and then ends with "Amen, amen, amen. Strike up the music! On with the dance." The grief as permanent weather pillar and the illusion as primary pillar converge here in a single liturgical form: the Christian ceremonies for the two great thresholds of human life, marriage and death, are revealed as structurally identical, which is Young's most honest theological claim. Both ceremonies ask the participants to stand before the irreversible and say words that acknowledge it and then continue. Both are performed by someone in a robe who does not know the participants personally. Both end with a meal. The difference between them is the direction of the transition, and Young's preacher, moving through both simultaneously, makes the direction seem less important than the ceremony itself, less important than the standing together in the face of what cannot be stopped.

"We were created by the dragonfly dropping upon its silken cable line. We were created by the images of the uncreated creation. We were created by a falling star singing as it fell. We were created by a shadow moving where the shadow increased." This is Mr. Spitzer's counter-Genesis, his alternative to "In the beginning God created," and it is the recursive construction pillar at its most theologically ambitious. Creation in Young is not a single act by a single author but an endless process of being-called-into-being by particular instances of beauty and contingency, the dragonfly, the star, the shadow. God's absence from this account is not denial but redistribution: the creative force is not concentrated in a single sovereign being but dispersed through every particular thing that has ever been beautiful enough or strange enough to make another being suddenly aware of existing. This is the theological claim the whole novel has been building toward, and it arrives not as argument but as list, as the same recursive accumulation by which Young constructs every truth the novel offers: not this or that explanation, but this and this and this and this, until the weight of the particular instances becomes its own kind of faith.

Movement Six: What the Novel Teaches

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · The Stone Deaf Man · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Dreams and Imagination

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Plato and Platonism

Allusions: Deafness and Sign Language · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · The History of Opium

Definition from research

The novel's last philosophical statement is delivered in two sentences: "Whatever is average is the dream. Whatever is hidden is the revealed." Vera speaks this near the end, reflecting on Miss MacIntosh, on the stone deaf man she has chosen to love, on the entire journey the novel has been on. They are not a resolution. They are the arrival at a paradox that has been building since page one, the paradox that is the AND at the center of Young's entire philosophical project: the ordinary and the extraordinary are not opposites. They are each other's deepest form.

Miss MacIntosh was the average. She was from What Cheer, Iowa, which she described as very ordinary, a small town like any other, where all but a few atheists went to church and they were very kind people, where the winters were cold and the children's ears were frozen and one broke through the frosty ground with a hoe. She was plain, practical, sensible, unremarkable in every way she insisted on being unremarkable. She was "the sensible and average and right." She was the dream. Vera did not understand this until the novel's end because the dream of a grounded ordinary life was what Vera most needed and least recognized, hidden in plain sight behind its own ordinariness. "Had I been less wrapped up in myself, I might always have known her, the other soul, its power, its enchantment."

The plural self pillar arrives at this paradox through characterization. Miss MacIntosh is not one person. She is the practical nursemaid and also the woman with a mastectomy and also the figure who walked into the sea and also the face of every face and the heart of every heart. But none of these other dimensions are available until you have accepted the plain surface first. Young spends the novel's opening chapters insisting on Miss MacIntosh's ordinariness with a kind of aggressive repetition that trains the reader to see her as she presents herself: common sense, flat feet, broken nose, the path of virtue rugged and hard. Only after that training has taken hold does the depth beneath the surface begin to emerge. The average conceals the dream. The ordinary is the door into everything Young is building, but it is a door that only opens if you approach it without impatience, without the desire to skip to the revelation.

Illusion as primary is where the reversal becomes most visible architecturally. Catherine's opium world is elaborate, populated, spectacular, inexhaustible in its invention. It is full of Platonists and drowned sailors and centaurs with lilies in their mouths. It is the opposite of average. And yet it is not the dream. It is the escape from dreaming, the place where the dreamer goes to avoid the dream the ordinary world contains. Catherine cannot bear the ordinary, which means she cannot bear the dream. She lives in a world of extraordinary illusions precisely because she has refused the average, and the refusal is what keeps her from the thing she most needs. What is hidden is the revealed: the truth about Miss MacIntosh, who she actually was, was hidden in her plainness all along. Catherine's spectacular phantoms are visible but opaque. Miss MacIntosh's plain fact is invisible but transparent, once you know how to look.

The grief as permanent weather pillar arrives at the paradox through the stone deaf man. He lost his hearing at fourteen in a sleep so near to death it might almost have been his death. He woke into silence. The human voice went first, then everything else, until there was only the memory of sound and a world of blurred shapes. He became a painter. He heard what others heard not, the fishes whispering at the bottoms of rivers. A butterfly made a loud noise wheeling around his head. He had traveled all over America and never heard a traffic horn, which is to say he had been spared everything ordinary about the noisy world and had been given instead a world of pure imagination in which silence was his permanent weather and everything he heard was internal. He is the novel's most extreme image of the hidden revealed: his deafness is the condition that reveals what hearing conceals, that the world is more beautiful and more strange than the traffic horn allows.

Vera's choice of the stone deaf man is not resignation and it is not settling. It is the application of the novel's final lesson. She has spent the entire book searching for Miss MacIntosh, for the ordinary world that Miss MacIntosh represented, the world of plain common sense where the dream was supposed to be absent. She arrives instead at the understanding that the ordinary world she sought was always already the dream, that Miss MacIntosh's plainness was itself the extraordinary thing, and that the man she loves is extraordinary precisely through his ordinariness transformed by loss into something else. He is the impossible artist who became a painter when sound died. He is the average, the stone deaf man swaying in a corridor at dawn, and he is also the dream.

The witness pillar closes the novel in the figure of the old Black woman who tells the newly deaf boy to dream on. Her speech is the only moment in the novel where Young gives a character the direct authority to name what the novel has been arguing: "life is imaginary, and this be an imaginary world." This is not nihilism. It is the statement that imagination is not the opposite of reality but its deepest form, that the world as it is and the world as it might become are made of the same substance, that the witness who attends fully to what is ordinary will find that what is ordinary is always also everything else. The Black woman in a racist America, speaking to a white boy whose deafness has placed him temporarily outside the protection his skin would normally provide, knows this from the inside of her own condition. Her suffering is different from his. The community they share is made of the fact that both are suffering what is not their fault, and in that shared condition she sees not tragedy but the beginning of imagination, which is the beginning of the world as it might become.

The recursive construction pillar is the device by which this final paradox lands with the weight it has accumulated across the entire novel. Young has spent 1,198 pages building toward "whatever is average is the dream" by showing us, again and again, the dream hidden in the ordinary: the honey in the skull, the bees that make the dead productive, the salt crystals bearding Miss MacIntosh's cheeks on the ordinary shore, the mute swan who does not sing even when it dies, the violinist who touched the strings only once. Each of these is a version of the same claim, deposited one after another into the reader's understanding until the claim has the weight of proof. The novel arrives at its final paradox not as a surprise but as a recognition, the sensation of having always known this without knowing that you knew it. That sensation is what Young spent sixteen years building. It is the deepest form of the ordinary. It is the dream.

Movement Five: The Traditions the Novel Absorbs

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Lucie Bell · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Eyes and Blindness · The Sea and Water · Weddings and Funerals

Allusions: Romantic Poets · The History of Opium · Women’s Suffrage

Definition from research

It is an ancient Mariner, / And he stoppeth one of three. / 'By thy long grey beard and

glittering eye, / Now wherefore stopp'st thou me?'

Samuel Taylor Coleridge, The Rime of the Ancient Mariner

The Compulsion to Tell

Coleridge's Ancient Mariner killed an albatross and brought disaster on his ship. All his crewmates died. He survived, cursed to wander and to retell the story of what he did to anyone he encounters, whether they want to hear it or not. The Mariner stops a wedding guest on his way into a wedding and holds him with his glittering eye and tells him everything. The wedding guest cannot move until the telling is complete. He misses the wedding. He rises the next day a sadder and a wiser man. This is the poem's formal structure: one who cannot stop telling, one who cannot stop listening, the wedding interrupted, the wisdom delivered at a cost.

Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is 1,198 pages long and cannot stop telling. This is not a formal failure. It is the poem's structural logic extended to novel length: the compulsion to retell the experience of catastrophic loss in full, without abbreviation, because abbreviation would falsify it. The Ancient Mariner tells the whole voyage. He cannot summarize. He cannot say: I killed an albatross and everyone died and I learned a lesson. He must tell every detail, every dead crewmate's eyes, every degree of the becalmed ocean, every water-snake he blessed. The novel does the same. Young cannot summarize Miss MacIntosh or the opium lady or Mr. Spitzer or the bus journey. The 1,198 pages are not excess. They are the formal requirement of the compulsion.

The Glittering Eye

Coleridge's Mariner stops people with his glittering eye. This is not a metaphor for compelling storytelling. In the poem it is literal and possibly supernatural: the eye holds the wedding guest against his will. He cannot choose to walk past. The eye fixes him.

The novel applies the glittering eye to Cousin Hannah: this old hunter with the glittering eye, the shining spear, the sword of ice. Cousin Hannah is the novel's most compulsive activist, the suffrage captain who cannot stop campaigning, who has ridden against great turbaned Turks and negotiated great torrents of ice and snow and deserts of stone, whose rage against man produces detonations still shaking the Cartwheel house after her death. She holds people with her argument the way the Mariner holds the wedding guest with his eye: not by persuasion but by some quality of the attention itself, a fixing that cannot be escaped.

The glittering eye appears twice more: once as a gospel salesman's glittering eyeballs before he converts a reeling woman in a doorway, and once simply as the hard glittering eyes of someone who faces the truth when she sees it coming. The glittering eye in the novel is always the eye of compulsion: the person who has something to tell and will not let you go until they have told it. The Ancient Mariner, Cousin Hannah, the gospel salesman, the truth-facer: all of them stopping people who are trying to get somewhere else and holding them with an eye that will not release.

Water Water Everywhere

The direct quotation appears in the hangman's chapter: Water, water everywhere, and not a drop to drink, he would say. The hangman has crossed the world on a yacht, imprisoning himself in it, keeping an extra plate at the dinner table for his sweetheart, feeding crumbs to invisible birds. He is a man who has done a terrible thing and cannot escape the knowledge of it. He has tried to escape by constant motion: travelling around the world, but he never saw it. The ocean surrounds him everywhere and he cannot reach it. The Mariner's becalmed curse is the hangman's condition: to move through water without being able to use it, surrounded by a world he has cut himself off from by what he has done.

The Mariner's curse is the novel's working description of guilt that has become a permanent atmospheric condition. Water, water everywhere: not a shortage but a surfeit, not deprivation but saturation. Too much of what should sustain you. The Mariner's ocean is not empty; it is full of rotting things, of dead crewmates, of the albatross hung around his neck. The hangman's ocean is the same: full of the weight of what he carries, of the extra plate, of the invisible birds he feeds because he killed the thing that should have been free.

The Albatross

At the novel's end, near the last pages, the word appears in a blues-inflected monologue: you'll hang around his neck like an albatross when you'll be gone. This is spoken to a woman named Lucie Bell who is leaving. The albatross is the burden of love that you carry after the thing you love is gone: not the living beloved but the memory of the beloved hanging around your neck, too heavy to lift off, a weight that marks you as the one who killed what should have been free.

This is the novel's deepest use of the Mariner structure. The Mariner kills the albatross out of impulse, without clear motive, and spends the rest of his existence carrying the consequence. He did not mean to destroy what he destroyed. Neither does anyone in the novel mean to destroy what they destroy. The opium lady did not mean to disappear into dreams and leave Vera without a mother who was present. Mr. Spitzer did not mean to survive Peron. Cousin Hannah did not mean to lose her one battle, the one against the opium lady's withdrawal. The Cartwheel house is full of people carrying albatrosses they did not mean to put on, hanging around necks that did not ask for the weight, marking them as the ones who were present when something beautiful died.

The Wedding Guest Who Misses the Wedding

The Ancient Mariner stops a wedding guest. The guest misses the wedding. He rises the next morning sadder and wiser. The wedding is not recoverable: while he was held by the eye and the story, the feast happened without him, the vows were said without him, the celebration that organized the day went forward without the one who was stopped on the threshold.

The novel's wedding passages enact this repeatedly. Cousin Hannah is the uninvited wedding guest who was sometimes ignored, sometimes frozen by the opium lady's remoteness, sometimes given a sidelong glance that might signify much or nothing. She is the one stopped at the threshold of the wedding that never quite happens: the marriage of the opium lady to her love, which is the love of a dead man, a shadow, a dream retreating at cockcrow. Cousin Hannah could not get in. She could not pull the opium lady out. She was stopped at the door of a wedding to a ghost, and she missed the ordinary life she was trying to pull her cousin toward, and she rose sadder and wiser from the encounter, and she died without having changed anything she tried to change.

The novel itself is the wedding guest's experience formalized. The reader is stopped at the threshold of ordinary time, held by the glittering eye of the narrative, told the whole voyage before being released. You rise from it sadder and wiser. You have missed, while reading, whatever wedding you were on your way to. That is the formal requirement. That is what the compulsion asks. The Ancient Mariner does not apologize for stopping you. The novel does not apologize for its length. The telling is the point. The stopping is the structure. The wisdom is delivered at the cost of the wedding, and the wedding, as the novel says, was always also a funeral.

Movement Five: The Traditions the Novel Absorbs

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Moses Hunnecker · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Death and Mortality · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Love

Symbols: Moon and Stars · The House · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Freud and Jung

Allusions: Astronomy · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Sir Walter Raleigh · The History of Opium

Chapters discussed: 9, 11, 13, 28, 45

Definition from research

She is gone, she is lost, she is found, she is ever fair. Sir Walter Raleigh, The Ocean's Love to Cynthia

The Entry Point: A Headless Visitor in Chapter 11

Sir Walter Raleigh appears in the novel exactly once by name, in Chapter 11, among the distinguished visitors Vera's mother receives in her opium-dream bedroom. He arrives in his historically documented seed-pearl suit. He removes his white plumed hat. He also removes his head. He asks to be addressed by his intimate name: Ocean or Water, for he had crossed many waters. He leads, as his head explains, a society of night devoted exclusively to atheistic propositions, such as that man had existed before Adam, and God is nothing but an idea in the mind, and God is dog spelled backward.

This is not a casual literary cameo. Every element is exact. Raleigh's nickname 'Water' was given to him by Elizabeth I, a pun on his name as it was then pronounced. He signed his letters to her as 'Water.' She was his Cynthia, his moon, his organizing principle, and he was her Ocean: the body that could not stop moving toward her. His great unfinished poem, written during his imprisonment in the Tower of London after Elizabeth discovered his secret marriage, was titled The Ocean's Love to Cynthia. The poem is 522 surviving lines of a work he never finished, a meditation on an ocean that has lost its moon, still moving, still pulled, still devoted to something that has withdrawn its light. The poem was written after disgrace. The execution came later, in 1618, seventeen years after Elizabeth's death. Young's Raleigh is headless: already past the end of his story, still carrying it.

The atheism detail is also precise. Raleigh convened what his enemies called the School of Night, a circle of heretical inquiry that included Christopher Marlowe, George Chapman, and others. They were accused of denying God, of asserting that Moses was a conjurer, of investigating the soul. Young's Raleigh leads his society of night from inside the opium lady's bedroom, which is also a kind of Tower of London: the place of confinement where the most dangerous thinking happens, where the exiled self keeps writing its unfinished poem.

The Poetic Chain: Marlowe, Raleigh, Williams

There is a three-part poetic exchange that runs through Chapter 13 and forms one of Miss MacIntosh, My Darling's deep literary architectures. Christopher Marlowe wrote The Passionate Shepherd to His Love, an invitation to an idealized pastoral existence: come live with me and be my love. Raleigh wrote The Nymph's Reply to the Shepherd, an almost line-by-line refutation: the flowers fade, the rivers rage, the honey dries, time drives the flocks from field to fold. No, the nymph says. Youth fades. Your promises are not adequate to what time does.

Raleigh's reply is the AND Philosophy's Act Two in crystalline form: the clear-eyed exposure of the illusion. It strips the pastoral fantasy of its timelessness. It does what Miss MacIntosh does: it points to the plain fact underneath the beautiful promise. But The Ocean's Love to Cynthia is something else entirely. It is not Act Two. It is Act Three attempted and abandoned. In that poem Raleigh knows that the pastoral was an illusion, knows that Cynthia has withdrawn, knows that he has been ruined, and keeps writing anyway. He cannot stop. The ocean does not stop moving because the moon has risen behind a cloud.

William Carlos Williams added a third term to the exchange in the twentieth century. His poem Raleigh Was Right opens: 'We cannot go to the country / for the country will bring us no peace.' Williams confirms Raleigh's refutation: the pastoral is not available. The country is not an escape. There is no going back to the idealized elsewhere. But Williams says this as a modern poet, after industrialization has made the pastoral not just philosophically hollow but geographically inaccessible. He has been agreeing with Raleigh across three centuries. The conversation is ongoing. It does not resolve.

This three-part exchange is the architectural spine underneath the novel's treatment of What Cheer, Iowa. Miss MacIntosh comes from What Cheer: a name that is itself a refutation of the pastoral. What cheer? Not much. She carries the plain Midwestern interior as her credentials against illusion. She is the Nymph's Reply embodied: no, the roses fade, the rivers are just rivers, the time is what the clock says. But she drowns in the ocean anyway. The ocean has the last word, as it always does in Raleigh's unfinished poem.

The Novel as Unfinished Poem: Ocean Imagery as Architecture

The preface to the novel tells us directly: Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is written with oceanic music moving at many levels of consciousness and perception. It also tells us: if one is to follow the full swelling of the wave of imagination one must bring back to the shore the wave which carried you. The novel does not describe an ocean. The novel is structured as one. What the Raleigh thread reveals is that this ocean structure is not a metaphor Young invented. It is an inheritance: the great unfinished poem of devotion to something that no longer governs you, still moving, still tidal, still pulling toward the shore that is not there.

The Moon and the Ocean: Gravitational Devotion

The key to the Cynthia/Ocean dynamic in the novel is not romance. It is gravity. The moon does not choose to pull the ocean. The ocean does not choose to be pulled. This is devotion that is structural, not willed: the most honest kind, and the most pitiless. The novel returns to this configuration across its entire length.

Chapter 9: the moon is described as invulnerable to our assault, the moon which draws the waves in its wake and has no life of its own. This is the Cynthia figure exactly. Elizabeth governs Raleigh not through will but through what she is. She does not choose to pull him; it is gravitational. And the moon has no life of its own: it is reflective, not generative. The queen is a surface. The ocean is the one doing the moving, the one with the interior life, the one suffering.

Chapter 9 again, later: Miss MacIntosh's head becomes chalk-colored as the dead moon which draws, in collaboration with all the planets, the spring tide in its wake. The dead moon governs more powerfully than the living one. After Miss MacIntosh disappears into the ocean, she becomes a governing absence. The tides of the novel's consciousness keep moving toward her even when she is gone. This is the exact situation of The Ocean's Love to Cynthia: written after disgrace, still addressed to the moon that has withdrawn.

Chapter 28: if the moon had lost its power to pull the tide. Mr. Spitzer wonders about this not as a catastrophe but as a kind of relief. What would it be like not to be pulled? He cannot imagine it. The inability to imagine it is the whole of The Ocean's Love to Cynthia. Raleigh keeps writing toward a queen who is no longer listening. He cannot stop. He does not finish. The poem ends in a fragment because the pull does not end.

Chapter 45: Mr. Spitzer was not the master of the tides, the scallop moon drawing the waves. This is the novel's clearest statement of the Cynthia principle applied to Mr. Spitzer, the novel's central consciousness across its later chapters. He is water. He is pulled. He did not choose this and cannot alter it. The question the novel asks of him is not whether he can stop being the ocean but whether he can do anything generous with that condition.

The House and the Ocean: Mourning as Architecture

The Cartwheel house has its back to the ocean. Vera's mother has black curtains facing the ocean. She is in mourning for the ocean. This spatial arrangement is one of the novel's most compressed AND Philosophy statements. The house turns away from the very thing it is built next to, which is also the thing that determines everything about it: the salt air, the damp, the tidal rhythm, the light off the water. Mourning for the ocean while living beside it: this is not a contradiction in Young's world. This is the accurate description of what it is to grieve a constitutive loss.

In Raleigh's poem, the ocean mourns Cynthia while Cynthia is still in the sky. The withdrawal of favor is not the same as disappearance. The moon is still there. The ocean can still be pulled. But the relationship is over, and the ocean keeps moving anyway, oriented toward something that no longer acknowledges it. The house with its back to the ocean is doing the same thing: maintaining its orientation in relation to what it has turned away from. The back of a house still knows where the ocean is.

Miss MacIntosh maintains the house's relationship to the ocean in an opposite and equally revealing way. She talks as if they are at sea constantly: all hands must be on board, we must plow the ocean, heave ho my hearties, all hands to the ropes. She has never been to sea. She wears a bathing suit she cannot swim in. She stands at the edge of tidal pools with her black umbrella. She uses the ocean as a metaphor for domestic routine while being constitutionally unable to enter it. This is the Nymph's position: knowing the ocean is there, refusing the pastoral invitation to dissolve into it, maintaining the plain dry shore of common sense against the pull. And then she walks in.

The Ocean Floor: We Were What We Mourned

The novel's most devastating ocean passage occurs in Mr. Spitzer's long insomniac section, where his consciousness is described as water-logged, sinking, submerged. All souls sink to the ocean's floor. Then: we mourned, not knowing that we were what we mourned, that we were on the ocean's floor.

This is the AND Philosophy's pillar of the plural self taken to its furthest reach. We are not separate from what we are grieving. We are not observers of the loss; we are inside it, on its floor, part of its sedimentation. Raleigh's poem makes the same move: the ocean does not look at itself from outside. The ocean is the grieving. In the novel, the ocean floor is not a destination but a condition. You are already there. You have been there. The mourning is not for something you have lost but for what you are.

The passage continues: if all were lost, how could one be lost? This is the logical conclusion of the ocean-as-universal-condition argument. If every soul is on the floor, then the floor is also the world. There is no above from which one could fall. The novel's oceanic structure is not an image of drowning but of already having drowned, which turns out to be the same as living. The ocean floor is where the novel lives.

Miss MacIntosh's Death: The Nymph Enters the Ocean

The sun and the moon shone in the same pearly sky when she walked into the ocean. This sentence, one of the most formally precise in the novel, appears twice in the Miss MacIntosh death passage. The doubling is not accidental. Sun and moon in the same sky: the time of day and the time of night simultaneously present, which is the condition of the novel at all times, which is also the condition of any consciousness holding the living and the dead together without separating them.

Miss MacIntosh is the Nymph throughout the novel: the one who says no to the pastoral invitation, no to illusion, no to the dissolving of the self in oceanic dreaming. She is the reality principle dressed in a black bathing suit. And she walks into the ocean. She gives herself to the undertow. The Nymph's Reply, that careful refutation, ends with the body entering exactly what it refused. Raleigh was right: the country will bring us no peace. But we go anyway. We cannot help it. We are pulled.

After her death, Vera sees the ocean differently. For Miss MacIntosh, the ocean would be safe, the best place for the keeping of treasures, of pearls. No harm could come from the sea if one lay under it. For Vera, it is the beautiful malignancy of always moving waters. This reversal is the novel's deepest AND Philosophy move. When the moon is gone, the ocean sees itself clearly for the first time. The thing that organized the consciousness by pulling it is no longer there, and the consciousness discovers it is still moving. The grief is not about Miss MacIntosh. The grief is the movement itself, recognized now for what it always was: the ocean's own nature, not borrowed from anything else.

Oceanus: The Ship That Sank with the Evening Star

Among the catalog of lost ships in the novel is one named Oceanus: plates of gold, Oceanus which sank with the evening star, rose not with the morning star though the captain gave good hope. In Greek cosmology, Oceanus was the primordial river encircling the world, the source of all waters. In the novel's lost-ships catalog, Oceanus is one wreck among many, failing to rise with the morning star despite hope.

This is Raleigh's poem compressed to a single image. The evening star and morning star are both Venus: one name for the same planet seen at different times of day. The ocean sinks with the evening star and does not rise with the morning star even though the captain gave good hope. The captain gave good hope: Raleigh gave the queen everything, kept faith, waited, gave hope. It did not rise. The ship's name is the thing it could not survive being.

The AND Philosophy Reading: What the Ocean Thread Does

The Ocean's Love to Cynthia thread is not a source study. It is a demonstration of how the AND Philosophy's five pillars operate at the level of formal structure, not just content.

The plural self: the ocean is not a single body of water. It is every body of water simultaneously, every consciousness that ever moved toward something it could not stop moving toward. Mr. Spitzer and Vera and the opium lady and Miss MacIntosh are all aspects of the same ocean: different surfaces, the same gravitational condition.

Illusion as primary: the pastoral of Marlowe's shepherd is the novel's clearest example of the beautiful lie. Come live with me and be my love: every character in the novel has been invited into some version of this. Every one of them knows the Nymph's Reply. All of them go anyway. The illusion does not become less operative when it is known to be an illusion. This is not failure. This is the constitutive condition.

Grief as permanent weather: Raleigh's poem is not a poem about having grieved. It is a poem written inside grief, still grieving, in the Tower, with no end in sight. The Ocean's Love to Cynthia is an unfinished poem precisely because grief of this kind does not arrive at a conclusion. The novel is structured the same way. It does not resolve. It accumulates. It keeps moving.

The witness: Vera is the novel's witness, watching the ocean, watching Miss MacIntosh, watching her mother watch the ocean with the curtains drawn. The witness is not outside the ocean; the witness is on the shore, which is also inside the ocean's reach. Every shore is the ocean's territory in weather. Vera's witnessing does not protect her from the tidal pull. It is the tidal pull: the inability to look away from the thing that has organized your life.

Recursive construction: the novel builds itself the way the ocean builds itself, by returning. Wave after wave covering the same ground, each pass slightly different, laying down sediment, uncovering it, laying it down again. Raleigh's poem returns to Cynthia obsessively, circling back to the same images of loss from different angles. The 1,198 pages of Miss MacIntosh, My Darling do the same thing. This is not repetition as failure. This is the ocean's formal logic.

The Unfinished Poem

The Ocean's Love to Cynthia was never finished. Whether Raleigh meant it as a fragment, whether he continued and the continuation was lost, whether imprisonment broke the sustained act of composition: we do not know. What survives is a poem that circles its subject without arriving, that names its grief without resolving it, that addresses a moon that is no longer listening in the same formal registers it used when the relationship was intact. It is the most honest love poem in the English language: honest because it does not pretend to be over, honest because it does not pretend to continue.

Young sets this poem inside her novel as its deep water. The novel's oceanic structure, its refusal to resolve, its devotion to characters who cannot stop moving toward what they have lost or never had: all of this flows from the same source. The ocean does not stop because the moon withdraws. The moon has no life of its own. The water has always been what was doing the moving.

Raleigh was right. We cannot go to the country. The country will bring us no peace. But the novel's last word on Miss MacIntosh is not this refusal. It is Vera, standing by the ocean she has always feared and never understood, watching the waves she cannot stop watching, asking: shall I not always remember her? The answer is built into the question. The tide draws the question out whether the question wants to go or not. It was never a choice.

Movement Six: What the Novel Teaches

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · The Stone Deaf Man

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Deafness and Sign Language · Music and Composers

Definition from research

There is a figure who recurs in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling with the insistence of a motif and the weight of a philosophical position: the impossible artist. Mr. Spitzer catalogues them in a passage of extraordinary compression: "the blind train conductor, the blind signalman signalling to the blind man, the deaf musician, the deaf conductor of the mute orchestra, the blind portrait painter or he who painted portraits only in water changing its conformation as he painted, perhaps when a bird flew over head, the blind lighthouse keeper with his light shining both by day and by night, seeming a sunken star, star and its ripple, the crippled dancer dancing in the wind, the mute swan singing not even when it died." He is drawn to them magnetically, he says, more than to any other category of human being. This is not sentiment. It is an architectural necessity. The impossible artist is the figure through which Young builds her deepest claim about what art is for and what the novel itself is doing.

The impossible artist is not someone who overcomes a limitation. That would be an inspirational narrative, which is not what Young is writing. The impossible artist is someone who creates from inside a condition that structurally prevents the creation, and whose work is therefore most pure precisely because it cannot be executed in the ordinary way. The blind portrait painter paints in water: each portrait is completed and then immediately unmade by the movement of the medium, altered by a bird flying overhead, returned to formlessness by the current. The painting exists for the moment it is made and then it is gone, but it was made. The mute swan does not sing even when it dies: the song that is supposed to be its greatest utterance never arrives, and the silence is the utterance. The violinist without arms cannot play, which means every performance he imagines is more perfect than any performance he could give.

The most elaborated instance of the impossible artist in the novel is a man Mr. Spitzer encounters who spent twenty years as a second violinist in the Philadelphia Symphony without once touching his bow to the strings. He played beside the other musicians, moving his bow with "the utmost mathematical precision, the most delicate gestures and knowledge of music," creating "the illusion of music where no music was." He was never discovered. The great conductor complimented him, pointed to him as the perfect example. Then one day, absent-mindedly, "prompted by his instinct for self-destruction, for failure," he touched the strings. He was immediately dismissed. "Was it right that for one false note, he should be driven forth, even as an Ishmael among men—that he should beg upon the streets?" The question is not rhetorical. Young means it. Twenty years of perfect silence, of music so precisely not-played that it was indistinguishable from playing: this is the impossible artist at his most extreme. The one note that ended his career was the only note that was real.

Mr. Spitzer himself is the novel's central impossible artist: a deaf composer of unwritten music. He writes his silent music on his shirt cuff, composing nocturnes, elegies, fugues "without instruments or voices," arranging migratory birds in their patterns of flight into musical notation on an imaginary scale that has no lines. He writes "a dirge for a dead clam, an evening sonata to a dead ear." The music cannot be heard because he cannot hear it and because it has never been performed and because the instruments and voices it requires do not exist in the world of sound. It exists fully, however, in the world of the novel.

The plural self pillar illuminates what the impossible artist means architecturally. Mr. Spitzer's deafness does not prevent his composition; it transforms its nature. He hears with "a deaf man’s memory of sound," which is to say he hears every sound he has ever heard, preserved intact because no new sound can displace it. The deaf composer's inner world is more densely musical than any hearing composer's, because nothing in it is competing with the external world. The impossible artist does not compensate for the missing faculty. The missing faculty becomes the source. The blind portrait painter cannot be distracted by what the face actually looks like. The violinist without arms cannot be betrayed by technique. The mute singer cannot be limited by what her voice can produce. Each impossibility strips away the interference between the inner vision and its expression, leaving only the vision.

The grief as permanent weather pillar runs through the impossible artist in the form Young gives him: he is always also the survivor. These are "old cripples who had been the kings of speed, or thought they had, and that was the same thing at certain levels of debate." The footless dancer was once a dancer. The blind portrait painter once saw faces. The stone deaf man at the novel's end "could remember how he had drifted into sleep and what were those last sounds he heard—the clatter of the moon vines upon an old, rotted porch—the far baying of a dog—the long white curtains blowing in the wind." The impossible artist carries the permanent weather of what was lost inside the condition that replaced it, and the work is made from both: from the memory of the faculty and from the transformation of its absence into something else.

The recursive construction pillar is where the impossible artist becomes the novel's formal argument about itself. Young spent sixteen years writing a 1,198-page novel in a literary culture that had no adequate framework for receiving it. The novel was too long, too dense, too uncompromising in its refusal to summarize. It was, in the terms of its own central motif, an impossible work. The violinist who never touched his strings had "succeeded even beyond his own wildest dreams" by creating the illusion of music where no music was. Young created the illusion of a conventional novel's readability, its forward movement, its character and plot, while actually building an entirely different kind of structure underneath, a philosophical architecture that becomes visible only after you have spent enough time inside it to understand what the walls are made of. The novel appears to be doing one thing and is doing another, like the Philadelphia violinist, for twenty chapters, fifty chapters, a hundred chapters, until the reader has learned to hear what is actually being played.

Young said she asked her writing students to attend not to what a work stated but to what it enacted. The impossible artist is what the novel enacts about itself: that the work most worth doing is the work that cannot quite be done by the instruments available, that the gap between the vision and the execution is not failure but the space in which the most honest art lives. Mr. Spitzer's silent music will never be performed. It is nonetheless composed. That it exists only in the novel, unheard, written on a shirt cuff beside the horse scores his dead brother kept, is not a limitation. It is the form that its truth requires.

Movement One: The Wheel Itself

Definition from research

Boethius wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison while awaiting execution. Lady Philosophy appeared to him and explained, among other things, the nature of Fortune: that she turns her wheel as she pleases, that the high are brought low and the low raised up, and that this turning is not cruelty but the fundamental condition of temporal existence. The wheel does not break the wise person because the wise person does not mistake Fortune's gifts for permanent possessions. What rises must fall. What falls was always going to fall. The wheel keeps turning whether we watch it or not.

Marguerite Young knew this work. She knew the medieval literary tradition that carried it forward, through Chaucer, through the mystery plays, through the long river of Western letters that treated the Wheel of Fortune not as a metaphor but as a diagram of how time actually works. She built that diagram into Miss MacIntosh, My Darling from the first page to the last, not as decoration or allusion, but as architecture. The Wheel is not something Young refers to. It is something she constructs the novel around, turning it through each of her five philosophical pillars until the wheel and the novel become indistinguishable from each other.

The clearest sign that this is structural rather than ornamental is that Young encodes it in the narrator's name before the novel properly begins. Vera Cartwheel. The name announces the novel's central preoccupation before a single chapter has unfolded: Vera, from the Latin for truth, attached to a wheel. Truth is a wheel. It turns. It does not stay. The self that seeks truth is herself part of the turning, cannot step outside it to observe from a safe distance, cannot stop the wheel to get a better look. Young names her narrator after the problem the novel is going to spend 1,198 pages not solving, because the Wheel of Fortune is not a problem that gets solved. It is the condition within which everything else happens.

The plural self is where the wheel does its most obvious work. In the Boethian framework, Fortune's wheel is impersonal: it does not turn for you specifically, it simply turns, and you happen to be on it. Young extends this logic inward. The self is not a fixed point around which fortune revolves; the self is itself multiple, turning, constituted by contradiction. When Vera observes that life must always have "these double motions like the progressions of delicate planets, circles within circles, wheels within wheels, orbs within orbs," she is not describing the external universe. She is describing the interior one. The self contains its own wheels within wheels, its own orbits that do not resolve into a single center. Mr. Spitzer is the clearest embodiment of this: he is always between two streams, unable to decide which way to turn, "undecided which way to turn, unable to stand still," his identity perpetually suspended in the moment before the wheel completes its revolution. The plural self is not a philosophical position Young's characters hold. It is the mechanical condition they cannot escape because they are made of the same stuff as Fortune's wheel: turning, multiple, never arriving.

Illusion as primary takes the Wheel of Fortune and asks what we actually see when we watch it turn. The rusted ferris wheel appears early in the novel, standing against a sky in a neighborhood of extreme poverty, and Vera observes that it "might be only a circle of sea birds." This is not whimsy. It is Young's epistemological claim: the wheel we see is always also something else, always already transformed by the perceiving mind into something the mind needs it to be. The ferris wheel rusted against the poverty sky is the Wheel of Fortune stripped of its grandeur, turned mundane and corroded, and yet still capable of becoming birds, becoming motion, becoming something other than what it materially is. Mr. Spitzer's watch, that jeweled instrument that marks "the hours, the minutes, the seconds, the days, the nights, the years, the revolutions of the planets around the sun," is itself described as "a starry wheel," making the measurement of time and the celestial mechanics of time into the same object, collapsing the practical and the cosmic into one thing held in one hand. Illusion is not the opposite of the wheel's turning. Illusion is how we survive the turning, the layer of perception that translates raw cyclical fate into something livable, something temporarily meaningful, something we can call home before the wheel takes it away.

Grief as permanent weather is where the Wheel of Fortune finds its emotional grammar in the novel, and Young is precise about this. In Boethius, Fortune's wheel produces grief because we attach to what it gives us and mourn when the wheel turns and takes it back. Young does not disagree with this, but she goes further: the grief does not end when we learn detachment. The grief is structural. The wheel broken at the cistern, an image drawn from Ecclesiastes into the fabric of the novel, names the grief not as a response to loss but as a permanent condition inscribed in the universe itself. The golden bowl broken. The wheel broken. These are not events that happened once. They are the description of how things are. The bus-driver's endless rounds through rain and darkness, his fat shoulders sloping over the wheel as he sleeps and drives, are not a metaphor for a life that once had meaning and lost it. They are the image of consciousness itself continuing after the wheel has broken, continuing because it has no other option, because the turning does not stop simply because the mechanism is rusted and the amusement park is empty and nobody is watching. Grief as permanent weather means the wheel keeps turning even when everyone has gone home.

The witness is the pillar that makes the Wheel of Fortune philosophically bearable in Young's architecture, and it operates here through the distinction between the wheel of chance and the wheel of cosmic order. Mr. Spitzer explicitly distinguishes between them: "the only implacable law was the divine law, the heavenly harmony, that which kept the planets in their course, that which controlled, with mathematical accuracy, the falling stars, the music of the spheres, the silent music, that which was not based on the roulette wheel stopping or games of chance, such as the marked cards, the loaded dice." His dead brother Peron had given himself to "the wastrel wheels of chance, the games of loaded dice, the croupiers," and it destroyed him. The witness does not play the roulette wheel. The witness observes the larger turning, the one that cannot be cheated, the one that produces the silent music rather than the noise of the gambling hall. This is not detachment in the Buddhist sense; it is a different quality of attention, one that can hold the wheel in view without trying to stop it, without betting on where it will land, without requiring the wheel to validate the self that is watching. The witness position is what allows grief to be permanent weather rather than permanent crisis.

Recursive construction is where Young's deployment of the Wheel of Fortune becomes most formally ambitious. The great potter who is looking the other way when some of them are turned upon the wheel, watching a flight of red-winged blackbirds instead of attending to his work, is one of the novel's most devastating images of how creation proceeds: not through deliberate intention but through recursive inattention, through the wheel turning while the maker's gaze is elsewhere. The wheel of blackbirds that becomes a wheel of stars that turns with the turning sun or moon, appearing in the bus-driver's dying vision, is the novel's formal logic made visible: one wheel becomes another becomes another, each image recursively generating the next, the turning structure reproducing itself at every scale from the cosmic to the creaturely. Madge and Homer are on the bus leaving the “dust-colored pottery town”. Madge is distressed over her pregnancy and that Homer “was not shaped by the great potter”. Madge insisted she would have been happier if “she had married the great potter”. Madge recalls the warning “He told me that all were clay, all men and some women.” The wheels within wheels of Catherine Cartwheel's father's factories and the wheels within wheels of the "hidden being" of the feminine nature and the wheels within wheels of the planetary progressions are not separate images. They are the same image at different magnifications, the novel's recursive architecture demonstrating through form what it argues through content: that the Wheel of Fortune is not one wheel but an infinite series of wheels turning within each other, each containing and generating the others, with no original wheel at the center and no final wheel at the edge.

Miss MacIntosh herself, the novel's emblem of stubborn linearity, who approved of nothing "outside of nature's wheel, though it should be a wheel casting foam and spray," is the figure against whom all this turning is measured. Her shoulders at the wheel, helping those who were not the children of fortune. Her straight back. Her plain sense. Her refusal of the infinite. She falls off the wheel entirely when her wig comes off and her bald head is revealed, and the novel never recovers from this, because the novel was always secretly about what happens when the one person who seemed immune to Fortune's turning turns out to have been turning all along, secretly, under her hat, the whole time. The wheel does not exempt the sensible. The wheel does not exempt anyone. That is Boethius's point. That is Young's point. They are, in this novel's long, turning argument, the same point.
