Quest Traditions Across Four Thousand Years in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling

All chapter references in this document are drawn from direct search of the novel. Where a quest work or figure is identified, the chapter number and passage are given. Interpretive claims are labeled as such.

I. The Frame

Vera states the novel's quest in the first chapter, plainly:

What motive in this quest but the search for life, for love, for truth that does not fail?

This is the frame within which every other quest in the novel operates. Vera's search for Miss MacIntosh, for What Cheer, Iowa, for the stable center of a world organized around practical facts and sensible shoes, is the surface quest. Beneath it, the novel holds nearly every major quest tradition in Western and some Eastern literary history, reaching back approximately four thousand years from Vera's bus journey through Indiana to an Egyptian sailor who arrived in Boston going the wrong way.

A direct search of the novel reveals a more complex architecture: six named literary quests, a second tier of archetypal wandering figures who are not literary titles but named presences in the book, and a structural argument about what quest means that the novel makes through its ending rather than stating outright.

II. The Foundation: The Egyptian Sailor

The oldest quest narrative embedded in the novel appears in Chapter 2, in Catherine's opium world. A drowned Egyptian sailor, gold-turbaned, his face glistening like clouded water, arrives in Catherine's bedroom. He has sailed from Egypt toward New York, gone off course, and arrived instead in Boston. He is, in the novel's own words, looking for Mr. Spitzer, trying to locate him in space if not in time.

Catherine receives him and gives him instructions for finding Mr. Spitzer through the house. The instructions are themselves a quest: she describes a shifting landscape, the schools of faceless dolphins which should follow in his wake, the great birds with teeth, the stars not in their places. She tells him: He should not be afraid of the minotaur, for the minotaur would be afraid of him.

The house has become a labyrinth. Catherine has become the oracle at its entrance. The Egyptian sailor is Theseus given directions by a woman in an opium bed. And the figure he is seeking, Mr. Spitzer, may or may not be findable, in space if not in time.

The Story of the Shipwrecked Sailor is among the oldest narratives in the literary record, dating to Egypt's Middle Kingdom period, approximately 2000 BCE. In it, a sailor is shipwrecked on an island and must find his way home. Young's Egyptian sailor has also been shipwrecked by misdirection: his captain misread the stars, the winds, the auguries of soothsayers and of birds and of horses' heads. He has arrived in the wrong place and is searching for someone who exists in time rather than in space. This is the quest structure at its most ancient: the traveler who has gone off course, who is looking for something or someone in a world that does not organize itself helpfully, who must navigate by stars that have moved from their expected positions.

Young did not name the Story of the Shipwrecked Sailor. She placed the Egyptian sailor, and the instruction not to fear the minotaur, and the labyrinthine directions, and left the reader to hear the resonance. The foundation is the oldest layer. Everything above it is built on top.

III. The Six Named Literary Quests

Young named six quest works directly within the novel. They are distributed across different characters and different chapters, and they are not evenly distributed one per character. The distribution is given here as confirmed from the book.

Pilgrim's Progress: Miss MacIntosh's Book

Pilgrim's Progress is the quest work most deeply embedded in the novel's physical texture. Vera, the narrator, describes her reading habits: "I would begin at the beginning, reading straight to the end or skipping only a few passages, and sometimes I would begin at the end, reading straight to the beginning, working from redemption backward, perhaps skipping the same passages, and she would never seem to notice..." Bunyan's single-direction journey from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City is being read backwards and forwards simultaneously. The quest is being reversed even as it is being transmitted.

Miss MacIntosh also carries Pilgrim's Progress physically through the novel as one of her personal objects, alongside her black umbrella and her fishnet bag. When she disappears, the novel asks: where was her black umbrella, and where was her Pilgrim's Progress? Her copy is last seen waterlogged, swollen by the sea. The guide through the wilderness has been soaked by the same water that took Miss MacIntosh.

Don Quixote: Two Windmill Chasers

Don Quixote appears in Chapter 1 applied to Moses Hunnecker: Was he, after all, a bachelor, perhaps even some mad Don Quixote chasing windmills? The question is Vera's, asked of the bus driver she cannot quite read. He reappears in Chapter 65, where another character says of Miss MacIntosh: Chasing windmills. Miss MacIntosh had always been chasing windmills. The windmill is the emblem of Quixote's error: the giant that was always a windmill, the quest object that was always something more ordinary than the quester believed. Young gives this emblem to both Moses and Miss MacIntosh: the two figures who drive and anchor Vera's journey are both, in someone's assessment, chasers of windmills.

The Odyssey: Two Men Who Did Not Go

The Odyssey appears inverted in Chapter 5. Moses, in his interior monologue, identifies himself as Penelope, not Ulysses: he was Penelope weaving this web, not Ulysses who wandered over the wide seas, he just staying at home and minding his own business. Moses is the one who stays, who keeps the home fires, whose hair grows as Penelope's weaving grew: a perpetual maintenance rather than a journey. In Chapter 23, Mr. Spitzer observes that Ulysses, if ever he had seen Penelope under electric lights, would never have come home. The Odyssey's homecoming is refused: the destination, seen clearly, is not worth arriving at.

Childe Roland: Catherine's Search

Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came, Robert Browning's poem of a knight who searches through a blasted landscape for a tower whose purpose he does not know, appears in Chapter 30 in the context of Catherine's long search for her lost husband Jock. Mr. Spitzer reports that Catherine implored Cousin Hannah to search for him in dark valleys, search for him where Childe Roland had blown his horn before a dark tower and where no other sound had ever been heard. The Dark Tower quest is the quest whose object is unknown even to the quester: Roland does not know what he will find or do when he reaches the tower. He finds it and blows his horn and the poem ends. Catherine's search for Jock has the same structure: she does not know what she would do if she found him. The quest is the motion, not the arrival.

The Divine Comedy: Mr. Spitzer's Self-Placement

In Chapter 29, in the middle of his long meditation on death and the body and his dead twin, Mr. Spitzer asks: "Or when should he come to the last infernal circle of this Divine Comedy of life and death?" He places himself explicitly within Dante's structure. His life is the Divine Comedy. He is descending through the infernal circles. The last circle is where he is headed. In the Inferno the last circle is the frozen lake of Cocytus, where the worst betrayers are embedded in ice. Mr. Spitzer does not elaborate on what his last circle contains. He asks when he will reach it. The question mark does its work.

The Holy Grail and Jason and the Argonauts: Cousin Hannah

Cousin Hannah receives both the Holy Grail and Jason and the Argonauts in Chapter 42, applied in the same passage: “she had not found the Holy Grail or any object of her quest. She was that Jason who had not found the golden fleece.” Both quest objects are withheld from her. The Holy Grail is the Christian quest object, the cup that holds the blood of Christ; the Golden Fleece is the pagan quest object, the impossible prize that Jason pursued across the known world. Cousin Hannah pursued suffrage for women with the same total commitment that heroes pursued these objects. She did not find either. The sheath had outlived the sword. Young gives Cousin Hannah both the sacred and the classical quest tradition, and both end the same way.

IV. The Second Tier: Archetypal Wanderers

Beyond the six named literary quests, the novel populates itself with archetypal quest figures who are not literary titles but named presences: wanderers who have been going for so long that they have become types rather than characters.

The Wandering Jew

Ahasuerus, the Wandering Jew or, as Catherine preferred to think of him, the Everlasting Jew, appears in Chapter 40 as one of Catherine's opium visitors. He is the figure condemned to wander until the Second Coming, having turned Christ away from his door on the road to Calvary. Catherine listens to him for hours. The Wandering Jew is the oldest Christian quest figure: not someone searching for something, but someone condemned to perpetual motion as punishment, unable to stop, unable to arrive. He is the anti-pilgrim: Pilgrim's Progress reaches the Celestial City; Ahasuerus never reaches anything.

The Northwest Passage

Chapter 32 contains the novel's most direct statement about the universal structure of the quest: For every soul must know finally its Northwest Passage, must find that which cannot be found, the crevice narrow as a thread suddenly opening into those great abysses filled with cities of frozen pinnacles and towers. The Northwest Passage is the quest that killed its questers for centuries: the sea route through the Arctic that explorers searched for and died searching for. Young's use of it here is precise: "For every soul must know finally its Northwest Passage, must find that which cannot be found, the crevice narrow as a thread suddenly opening into those great abysses filled" Not find. Know. The finding is not the point. The knowing of the impossibility is what the quest produces.

Polar Explorers and the Real Questers

Admiral Peary, Shackleton, and the polar expedition tradition appear repeatedly across the novel, most densely in Miss MacIntosh's geography chapters, where she asks Vera: Where is Shackleton Shelf, Enderby Land, Keeling Islands? The polar questers are the ones who went to the edges of the known world and came back having failed to reach the pole, or having reached it and disputed whether they had, or having died on the ice. Cousin Hannah is described as a great balloonist and mountain-climber in the same tradition. Her suffrage quest and the polar quests are held in the same breath because they have the same structure: the journey to an extreme, the attempt to plant a flag at the furthest point, the question afterward of whether anyone actually got there.

The Crusaders

The Crusader figure is applied specifically to Cousin Hannah across multiple chapters. She is that noble Crusader armored by her pride, the great beau sabreur of suffrage brandishing her sword. The Crusades were quests organized around recovering a holy city. Cousin Hannah's quest was organized around recovering the rights of women. Young makes the structural parallel explicit without apologizing for it: the Crusader who sets out to take Jerusalem and the suffragette who sets out to take the vote are both questers who organize their entire lives around a single object and pour everything into the motion toward it.

V. The Labyrinth at the Center

Catherine's instructions to the Egyptian sailor in Chapter 2 contain a structural argument about the novel's entire quest architecture that is worth reading slowly. She tells the sailor he must circle back the way he came, climb the stairs he has already descended. She tells him the doors have changed their places. She tells him not to fear the minotaur, for the minotaur would be afraid of him. The house through which she is directing him is a labyrinth, and the labyrinth does not have a stable architecture: the rooms between the rooms multiply, the doors relocate, the distance between one object and another is illusive.

The Minotaur at the center of the labyrinth is what Theseus was questing for: the thing to be slain at the destination. Catherine tells the Egyptian sailor not to fear it. She does not tell him it is not there. The minotaur exists. It is just afraid of him. The thing at the center of the labyrinth is afraid of the quester who has come all this way to face it.

What is at the center of this novel's labyrinth is the question the quest chapter cannot answer by counting quest references. It is the question Vera has been asking since Chapter 1. The search is for life, for love, for truth that does not fail. The minotaur at the center may be the truth that does fail. It may be Miss MacIntosh's baldness. It may be the realization that the stable center does not exist. Whatever it is, it is afraid of Vera. She has come far enough.

VI. The Ending: Bee Bak in a Whale

The novel's final lines are Esther Longtree's restaurant sign: “Owt to luntsch. bee bak in a whale. For she could not spell either.”

The sign is misspelled. Back is spelled bak. Whale is spelled whale but means while. Except that it also means whale. Jonah went into the whale and came back. The whale is the place of transformation between going and returning: you go in one person and come out another, if you come out at all. Esther Longtree has gone to lunch. She will be back in a while. She will be back in a whale.

The novel ends not with Vera's arrival at What Cheer, Iowa. She does not find Miss MacIntosh. The quest does not reach its stated destination. Instead the novel ends with a promise of return, misspelled, hung in a restaurant window in Indiana, signed by the woman who is the mother of us all and who cannot spell.

This is the quest's resolution. Not arrival. Not the object found. Not the golden fleece retrieved, the Holy Grail discovered, the Celestial City entered, the last infernal circle passed through. The resolution is a sign on a closed door that says: I have gone somewhere. I will come back. The quest continues. The restaurant is closed. Come back later.

This novel is one in which nothing concludes and everything begins over again. The Egyptian sailor is still in the house, waiting for Mr. Spitzer. The bus is still driving through Indiana. Moses's hair is still growing. Vera has arrived somewhere that is not What Cheer. She is going to be married and invite everything alive and dead to the wedding. Esther Longtree would be her. The sign on the door says she will be back in a whale.

Four thousand years of quest literature are gathered in this novel, from the shipwrecked Egyptian sailor reading the wrong stars to the stone deaf man Vera loves at the end. Every tradition Young drew on ends the same way: the quester finds something other than what they sought, and the finding is the quest's true content. What you were looking for was never the point. The looking was.

He had found an old woman who had been, in her youth, the greatest Lady Macbeth, though she had left the stage because of a nervous disorder, her conviction that she had killed Banquo, and for years had wandered from hobo camp to hobo camp, dressed as a man. Then one night, protecting her honor, defending herself against a man who had believed she was a man, she had killed him, shooting him with a rusted pistol. And she had drifted on, swearing like a drunken sailor, smoking a brown cheroot, perhaps

because of that one man she could not kill, that man who was herself.

The Play and Its Contamination

In Shakespeare's Macbeth, Lady Macbeth is the engine of the murder. Her husband wavers. She calls on spirits to unsex her, to fill her with cruelty, to stop the passage to remorse. She organizes the killing of King Duncan. She comes apart afterward: the sleepwalking, the compulsive handwashing, the cry that all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand. She kills herself offstage. The play does not show her death. She simply disappears from it while still alive, broken by the guilt she summoned the spirits to remove and could not finally remove.

Shakespeare's Lady Macbeth is entirely consumed by guilt for what she actually did. She organized a real murder. She cannot wash the blood off her real hands. Her madness is the return of the remorse she tried to block.

The novel's Lady Macbeth is consumed by guilt for what she only performed. She played the role. She was in her youth the greatest Lady Macbeth. And then the role became real to her: she left the stage because of a nervous disorder, her conviction that she had killed Banquo. Not that she had played the role of someone who killed Banquo. Her conviction that she had done it. The performance crossed into reality not through action but through belief. She became Lady Macbeth not by doing what the character does but by experiencing what the character experiences: the guilt that cannot be washed off, the conviction of murder, the nervous disorder that is the form remorse takes when it has no actual crime to attach to.

The Woman Who Became Her Role

She left the stage. This is the first crossing: from representation to belief. The stage is where you perform guilt for an audience and then go home. She could not go home. The guilt followed her out of the theater because it had become real to her, not as performance but as experience. The conviction that she had killed Banquo is not delusion in the clinical sense of having no connection to anything real. It is the actor's occupational hazard taken to its extreme: total identification with the character, the interior life of the role becoming indistinguishable from the actor's own interior life.

She wandered from hobo camp to hobo camp, dressed as a man. This is the second crossing: from guilt to disguise. Lady Macbeth called on spirits to unsex her: make thick my blood, stop up the access and passage to remorse, come to my woman's breasts and take my milk for gall. She asked to be made not-a-woman so that she could do what she needed to do without the passage to remorse that womanhood supposedly carried. The actress, living out the character's logic rather than the character's plot, enacts this unsexing literally: she dresses as a man. She passes out of the category of woman into the hobo camps, the rough male world, the cheroot-smoking drifting life. She has become Lady Macbeth's wish rather than Lady Macbeth's fate.

Then one night, protecting her honor, defending herself against a man who had believed she was a man, she had killed him, shooting him with a rusted pistol. This is the third crossing: from performance to actual act. She has now done what Lady Macbeth organized but did not personally execute. She has killed a man. The guilt that had been unearned guilt, guilt for a performance, guilt for Banquo who was never real, has now earned itself a real body. She has done, in her own person, in self-defense, the thing that destroyed Lady Macbeth from the inside.

That Man Who Was Herself

And she had drifted on, swearing like a drunken sailor, smoking a brown cheroot, perhaps because of that one man she could not kill, that man who was herself.

This sentence is the AND Philosophy's plural self at its most compressed and most violent. There is the man she could not kill: herself. The self she could not eliminate is gendered male in the syntax because she has been living as a man, has killed a man, has become through performance and disguise and actual murder something that the original female self could not have contained. She is a man who is also a woman who is also a character she played who is also a murderer who is also the guilty one who cannot wash her hands. She cannot kill the man who is herself because that man is also herself, and you cannot kill yourself without dying, and she has not died, she has drifted on.

Mr. Spitzer finds her in one of the hobo camps he visits in his wanderings among the derelicts. He catalogs her alongside a banker who did not know he was a banker, a lawyer who did not know he was a lawyer, a judge who did not know he was a judge, a cancer specialist who had not known he was a cancer specialist. All are people who have shed or lost or hidden the identity that the world assigned them. The Lady Macbeth actress is their logical extreme: not someone who has lost an identity but someone who has gained too many, who has crossed from one into another so many times that the original boundary is gone. She is not hiding. She is lost. She has too many selves stacked inside her: the woman, the actress, the character, the murderer, the man.

Shakespeare's Character Become Real

Lady Macbeth is a leading character in Shakespeare's play who goads her husband into regicide, becomes queen, is driven to madness by guilt, and commits suicide offstage. Young takes Shakespeare's character and allows her, through the medium of an actress, to complete the trajectory the play left incomplete.

Shakespeare's Lady Macbeth kills herself offstage and the play moves on to Macbeth's death at Macduff's hand. The guilt that broke her is not resolved, only ended. She exits the play through offstage death before the play reaches its conclusion. Young's actress-Lady Macbeth does not exit through suicide. She exits through transformation: she becomes a man, she kills a real man, she drifts on. She is still alive when Mr. Spitzer finds her. She has survived what Shakespeare's character could not survive, not because the guilt has been resolved but because she has accumulated so many selves that no single guilt can break the whole structure. She cannot wash the blood off Lady Macbeth's hands because she also has the hobo's hands and the man's hands and the killer's hands and the actress's hands and the woman's hands and none of them are the same hands.

The AND Philosophy Reading

The Lady Macbeth passage is the AND Philosophy's plural self demonstrated through the mechanism of theatrical possession. An actor does not become a character. An actor uses the character to discover what the character's experience would feel like from inside. The actress who was the greatest Lady Macbeth discovered, from inside, that the guilt felt real. This is not a failure of sanity. This is the actor's craft taken to its fullest and most dangerous extension: the complete inhabitation of an interior life that is not your own, which is also the AND Philosophy's definition of the witness. The witness inhabits what they are watching. The witness does not observe from outside. The witness feels from inside the thing they are witnessing. The actress who left the stage because she had killed Banquo was not deluded. She was witnessing from inside.

The grief as permanent weather pillar: she drifts from hobo camp to hobo camp because the guilt has no fixed location to attach to. The crime was performed. The conviction is real. The body count has now been made real in self-defense. But there is no house where she can go back to wash her hands. There is no offstage where she can exit. There is only the drifting, the cheroot, the swearing like a drunken sailor, the knowledge of that one man she could not kill.

That man who was herself is the novel's most concentrated statement of the self that grief and guilt and performance and disguise and actual action have produced: a self so plural, so accumulated, so built from crossings and survivals and transformations that it cannot be addressed as a single entity. She cannot kill the man who is herself. She cannot stop being the woman who is also that man. She drifts on. Mr. Spitzer finds her. He catalogs her. He moves on. She is still there, the greatest Lady Macbeth, in the hobo camp, in the cheroot smoke, in the space between the self she started as and the man she became and the self that survives them both.

Definition from research

Young said she did not want the novel to be seen as all doom and gloom, that there was a great deal of comedy in it. The statement has been largely ignored. The critical tradition around Miss MacIntosh, My Darling treats it as a cathedral of grief and philosophical weight, which it is, but this treatment misses something structurally essential: the comedy is not relief from the serious work. It is the serious work, operating through a different register. Young understood, as the best comic writers always have, that comedy is the form that takes the most seriously the gap between what things are and what they are supposed to be, and that this gap is precisely the territory the five pillars are built to inhabit. Grief as permanent weather requires comedy because without it the grief becomes sentimental, which is the one thing Young never permits. The witness requires comedy because the only way to sustain full attention to the world's contradictions without flinching is to find them funny as well as devastating. Illusion as primary requires comedy because the mechanism by which illusion operates, the straight face that insists on the impossible, is the mechanism of the joke.

The novel announces its comic method in one of its earliest and most sustained exchanges. The mother asks Mr. Spitzer: "Tell me, is there or is there not an invisible elephant in the corridor leading to this bedroom?" Mr. Spitzer, "smoothing his grey velvet cuffs, his mouth yawning, his eyes dimmed," maintains that "the burden of proof...rested not on him but on my mother who had seen the invisible." The mother's counter: why should an elephant rest on her, such a huge elephant, "a composition of sultry light beams, and with such a long memory, it could remember everything." And then the clincher: "Besides, if there was no elephant, then what was an elephant doing in the house?" This is not absurdism deployed to signal philosophical depth. It is a genuine comic argument about epistemology, about who bears the burden of proof for the invisible, structured as a perfect straight-man routine in which Mr. Spitzer is the straight man and the invisible elephant is the premise neither party will abandon. The exchange is funny because it is logically rigorous. The mother's final question, "what was an elephant doing in the house," is unanswerable within the terms of any epistemological framework Mr. Spitzer could bring to bear. She has won the argument by the rules of the argument.

The servants of the household have developed, through long proximity to the mother's opium world, a parallel universe of institutional comedy. One thinks he is waiting on Wellington because they have discussed Wellington so much. He is called Wellington by the other servants, and the mother asks him how Wellington is, what Wellington's appetites are, as though the conversation has always been about a third party who happens not to be present. Another servant thinks he lives in a forest of cuckoo clocks. One imagines he is Hannibal driving the elephants over the Alps. The second gardener thinks he is "a cosmic praying mantis reaching through miles of starlight." The servants dispute among themselves whether it is Roman in the morning or Greek in the afternoon. The blue room is already occupied by Plato's boat, et cetera. This is Young at her most fully comic, the "et cetera" doing exquisite work: having established that the household's rooms are assigned to historical and philosophical figures without regard for century, the prose waves away the rest of the list because to continue it would reduce the comedy by over-explaining it. The et cetera is the punchline's perfect punctuation.

Moses Hunnecker the bus driver is the novel's most comprehensively comic character, and his comedy is political satire delivered in a vernacular monologue that never stops, never quiets, and never for a moment loses the internal logic that makes it devastating. He will not cut his hair "until Roosevelt got out of the White House and all those Brain Trusters were busted with their W.P.A. projects and their public parks and their marble bird baths and their rotten roads and their free skating rinks that nobody wants when the river is frozen over and their free kindergartens that nobody wants." The list escalates from large to deliberately small, the marble bird baths arriving with the same indignation as the rotten roads, the free skating rinks positioned as culturally equivalent to governmental overreach, all of it delivered by a man driving a bus while drinking whiskey and invoking "God and all ye angelic choirs" in the same breath. Moses Hunnecker is a comic character in the Dickensian tradition: grotesque, exaggerated, completely himself, and in his very excess a precise portrait of a particular American type and a particular American political psychology. His hair, growing uncut as Roosevelt's terms multiply, is the novel's funniest physical gag and simultaneously a completely serious image of the body as political protest, of the personal as the political before that phrase existed.

The Christian hangman Mr. Weed and the landlord at the hotel provide the novel's most formally constructed comic exchange, a duet of professional non-sequiturs in which each man's area of expertise renders him unable to hear the other's. The hangman ties knots that end lives. The landlord ties knots that join lives. They discuss knots for several pages without either noticing they are talking about incompatible things. The hangman worries he nearly killed a dog. The landlord worries about ships that sink. The hangman wears his Sunday clothes to hangings and to church because they are the same occasion. The landlord notes that the hangman's bow-tie is loose: "Someone else will have to tie it. This is something a wife should do." The comedy is structural: two men in a late-night hotel room, each carrying the weight of his own mortality in the professional form it has taken for him, talking past each other with perfect comic timing across the gap that the plural self pillar names but cannot bridge. Their exchange is funny in the way that mortality is funny when you look at it directly enough.

The mute with the frog in his mouth is the novel's purest image of comedy as a philosophical method. The mute has trained a frog, through long practice and "labial and laryngeal and dental manipulations," to serve as his voice box, and in this capacity the frog has performed the Lord's Prayer in a thieves' café, advised on betting, and cautioned against pickpockets. When the frog dies, Mr. Spitzer attends its funeral in his "flowing black Englishman's bowtie and mourning cloak," because there is no one else to share the mute's grief. The comedy is completely earnest: Young is not laughing at the frog's funeral. She is presenting it with the same full dignity she extends to every form of grief and loss in the novel, which is itself the comedic method. The frog has served as a voice for someone who had none. That this is funny does not make it less true. The recursive construction pillar builds here as it always does: the absurd image contains within it a perfectly serious philosophical claim about what voices are, what they cost, and what it means to lose them.

Miss MacIntosh is funny in the way that total consistency is funny when it meets a world that refuses to be consistent. Her responses to the world's philosophical confusions are practical to the point of comedy: she dismisses chess as a game for kings and focuses on navigation and cooking, she prefers Pilgrim's Progress to the Word of God because Bunyan is "fairly safe even though not altogether trustworthy," she laughs wildly when a man at the Stock Exchange invites her to the North Pole with nothing but ear muffs, "her mouth wide and cavernous, a red ridge on her broken nose, her bald head sloping like a snowy cape." Miss MacIntosh laughing wildly on the Stock Exchange, bald, being invited to both poles simultaneously, is the novel's definitive image of what the witness pillar looks like when it is fully inhabited: clear-eyed, practical, absolutely itself, and completely capable of finding the situation hilarious without losing its grip on what the situation actually is.

Young knew that a novel about grief as permanent weather, about illusion as the primary mode of experience, about the plural self and the failure of identity and the impossibility of verification, had to be funny. Not to leaven its seriousness but because seriousness without comedy is sentimentality, and sentimentality is the one form of illusion Young refuses. The comedy is proof that Young was watching the world with both eyes open: one eye for what is devastating about it, and one eye for what is genuinely, structurally, unarguably absurd.

Definition from research

The preface to Miss MacIntosh, My Darling makes a striking defensive claim on Young's behalf: "Although she accomplishes for native American folklore the same immortality of the myth that Joyce accomplished for Ireland, Joyce was not her inspiration. Her inspiration was America." The defensiveness is telling. By 1965 the comparison to Joyce was both the most available compliment and the most limiting frame for any writer working at this scale of formal ambition, and the preface tries to redirect the conversation toward the American vernacular rather than the European modernist tradition. What neither the preface nor subsequent criticism has adequately addressed is the more fundamental question: not which tradition inspired Young, but what she does with tradition as such, how intertextuality functions in this novel not as allusion or homage but as primary construction method, the mechanism by which the recursive construction pillar actually builds.

The most shocking demonstration of this method arrives early, when Vera describes the bus journey through the Middle West: "We had passed a windmill, a leaning tower, Noah's Ark, the old woman who lived in the shoe." Noah's Ark and the Old Woman in the Shoe are not metaphors here. They are roadside buildings, pieces of rural American architecture dotting the landscape alongside coffee urns and wigwam nightclubs. Young has taken two of the most foundational intertextual resources of Western civilization, one biblical, one from the nursery rhyme tradition, and made them literal objects in the physical world of the novel, sitting alongside the melancholy buffalo tethered under a denuded oak and the faded washing on the line. This is the recursive construction pillar at its most methodologically explicit: the novel absorbs the entire Western literary tradition as material, refuses to keep it in the elevated register of allusion, and builds it into the ground-level American landscape as furniture. The sacred text and the nursery rhyme arrive in the same sentence, at the same scale, with the same grammatical weight. This is not irreverence. It is a structural argument about how all inherited texts function: as the architecture of the world we move through, as present and as ordinary as roadside buildings, available to be passed and noted and left behind.

Don Quixote appears early in the novel in exactly this flattened mode: Mr. Spitzer is "perhaps even some mad Don Quixote chasing windmills," and the windmill has already appeared in the landscape as literal roadside architecture two pages earlier. Young has the bus pass the windmill before she gives Spitzer the Quixote comparison, which means the intertextual reference arrives after the concrete object, reversing the usual direction: typically the object illuminates the reference, but here the physical windmill precedes the literary windmill, making the Cervantes allusion feel like recognition rather than elevation. Mr. Spitzer does not resemble Don Quixote because he is tragic and deluded; he resembles Don Quixote because the windmills are actually there, in the Middle West, just past the Ark and the shoe, and someone has to contend with them.

Pilgrim's Progress is the novel's most sustained intertextual structure, and it operates not as allusion but as inverted architecture. Miss MacIntosh prefers Bunyan to the Word of God itself, "fairly safe even though not altogether trustworthy as a guide through this great wilderness, this mortal life which was a path of thorns." Vera reads it to Miss MacIntosh, "sometimes I would begin at the end, reading straight to the beginning, working from redemption backward," which is the recursive construction pillar making its formal argument: the book that promises a linear progress from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City can be read backward, from redemption toward sin, and the journey is identical in either direction because Young's novel does not believe in linear progress. When Miss MacIntosh disappears, her Pilgrim's Progress is found "water-logged with marks of sea shells on its pages," left on the beach alongside her sea boots and broken umbrella. The book of Protestant virtue's end is not the Celestial City but the tide. Young gives Bunyan's pilgrim exactly the conclusion his own book refuses: dissolution into the sea, the body of water that throughout the novel represents everything Protestant plain-speaking cannot account for.

The inversion of classical epic is the intertextual operation Young performs most consistently through Mr. Spitzer. He is "Penelope weaving this web, not Ulysses who wandered over the wide seas, he just staying at home and minding his own business." The gender inversion here is not a feminist joke at Homer's expense. It is Young's structural claim about what the novel does with the epic tradition: the wanderer's role, the heroic quest, the return to Ithaca, these are all transferred to the absent figure, to Peron who has died and cannot return. The one who stays home, the one who waits, the one who weaves and unravels, he is the novel's consciousness, which means the novel's consciousness is Penelope's consciousness, the domestic intelligence that holds everything together in the absence of the adventurer. The Odyssey, filtered through this inversion, becomes not the story of a hero's journey but the story of the one left behind, which is the story the novel tells about grief.

The mother's canary exemplifies the most intricate intertextual architecture in the novel. She names her canary: Juniper, Tulip, Cellini, Solomon, Methuselah, Marco Polo, Admiral Peary, Shackleton, Dante. The list moves from flower to Renaissance goldsmith to biblical king to biblical patriarch to medieval explorer to polar explorer to medieval poet, covering five centuries and four continents in nine names applied to a single yellow bird that is, unbeknownst to her, actually many birds, each one secretly replaced when it dies. Young embeds the Ship of Theseus paradox inside the intertextual catalog: the bird that accumulates all these names is never the same bird, and the names that were given to one bird now apply to another, which means Dante the canary and Dante the poet share the same epistemological condition as the bird and the next bird: continuity asserted in the face of replacement, identity maintained by the refusal to acknowledge the substitution. This is what Young's intertextuality does structurally: it applies the names of the tradition to material that keeps changing underneath the names, and the names both illuminate the material and survive it, outlasting each particular instance of the thing they were attached to.

The literary dead appear in the mother's bedroom as houseguests: "crippled Mr. Alexander Pope, for example, he who had been scorned by Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, Lord Byron with his club foot, Shelley's bright hair like a comet in the wind, blind Milton dictating Paradise Lost to those indifferent daughters." Three of the four are identified by their physical impairments or personal humiliations rather than their literary achievements, and Paradise Lost arrives not as canonical text but as a domestic situation: a blind man dictating to daughters who do not care. Young does this throughout: the canonical text is always also a human situation, always embedded in a body with a club foot or a scorned love or a progressive blindness, always inseparable from the particular life that produced it. This is the plural self pillar applied to literary history: Pope is not only the author of the Essay on Man, he is the man Lady Mary Wortley Montagu did not love, and both are equally real, equally present in the room where Vera's mother is dreaming.

Virgil's "sunt lacrimae rerum," there are tears for things, arrives as the mother counts her pearls: "Sunt lacrimae rerum. But her tears were never for persons. To her, a human personality was a mere appearance, like a shadow upon the water." Young cites the Latin without translation, without footnote, as a fact in the prose the way the bus passes Noah's Ark as a fact in the landscape. The grief as permanent weather pillar is the translation: tears not for persons but for things, for the whole weight of existence rather than any individual instance of it, which is precisely what Young's grief-architecture requires. Virgil's line, from the Aeneid, is Aeneas weeping at the sight of a painting of the Trojan War in a foreign land, weeping because sorrow travels, because grief exceeds its origin, because the image of the dead persists in places the dead never reached. Young uses it to describe a woman who feels grief at the cosmic scale but cannot direct it toward any individual. They are the same grief, Aeneas's and the mother's, which is the claim recursive construction makes: all the grief in the tradition is one grief looking at itself in different mirrors across time.

"Although she accomplishes for native American folklore the same immortality of the myth that Joyce accomplished for Ireland, Joyce was not her inspiration." The preface is right that Joyce was not her inspiration, but it is wrong to limit her intertextual range to folklore. Young did for all of Western literary tradition what the American roadside did for Noah's Ark: made it a building you drive past on the way from here to there, present and weathered and ordinary and still, despite everything, the shape it always was. That is a different achievement from Joyce's. It may be a larger one.

Anatole France, William James, and the Philosophical Architecture of Miss MacIntosh, My Darling

There is a number that matters. Miss MacIntosh, My Darling runs to 1,198 pages. William James's Principles of Psychology, his 1,200-page treatise on the stream of consciousness, is the work Young named when she told interviewers whom she admired. The two-page difference is not rounding. Young spent eighteen years building this novel, controlled every sentence, and stopped where she stopped. She knew the number she was working toward.

This chapter argues that the architecture of Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is built on three interlocking foundations that have not previously been described as a unified structure: the philosophical method of Anatole France, the psychological scale of William James, and the unresolved tension between Epicurus and Plato that both France and the novel hold permanently open. Understanding this structure does not simplify the novel. It explains why the novel refuses to be simplified, and why that refusal is its most serious philosophical commitment.

I. The Garden: Anatole France and the Method of Irresolution

Marguerite Young was a reader of Anatole France. France was not merely a favorite; he was, for Young, a model of what literary philosophy could do when it refused to conclude. France won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1921, the same year he published a novel called Marguerite. He was known for his socialist sympathies, his wit, his deep skepticism of dogma in any form, and his extraordinary gift for holding incompatible ideas in the same hand without crushing either.

The work of France's that bears most directly on Miss MacIntosh is The Garden of Epicurus, a philosophical novel set in ancient Greece following Ariston, a young philosopher drawn to the teachings of Epicurus. But the novel is not an Epicurean tract. It is a staging of the encounter between Epicurean materialism and the persistent human longing that materialism cannot satisfy. France was, throughout his career, drawn to the transitional period between paganism and Christianity: the historical moment when a philosophy of the body and its pleasures met a philosophy of the ascending soul and neither could eliminate the other. He staged that encounter rather than resolving it. His garden is not a place of settled doctrine. It is a place where the argument continues.

France also inhabited the Platonic tradition, not as a believer but as an ironist who found the ladder of Eros both beautiful and unreachable. In The Revolt of the Angels, arguably his most philosophically dense novel, the fallen angel Arcade discovers that if he overthrew God, he would become God: the same trap wearing a different name. The lesson is not that revolution is wrong but that any system that replaces one authority with another has missed the actual problem. The actual problem is interior. France located it in the self's irresolvable desire for something it cannot name and cannot stop reaching toward. That desire has a name in Plato. It is Eros.

There is a third France novel that speaks directly to Miss MacIntosh, My Darling, and it is perhaps the most philosophically compressed of all his works. The Revolt of the Angels is often considered France's most profound and ironic novel. It tells the story of Arcade, the guardian angel of the bishop Maurice d'Esparvieu, who grows bored because the bishop is sinless, begins reading the bishop's books on theology, becomes an atheist, loses his wings when he falls in love, and joins a revolutionary movement of fallen angels. When the revolutionary movement finally encounters the Devil, the Devil realizes something that stops the revolution entirely: if he overthrew God, he would become just like God. The structure he was rebelling against would simply be reproduced under a new name. Arcade understands the lesson. Replacing one authority with another changes nothing unless, as France writes, in ourselves and in ourselves alone we attack and destroy Ialdabaoth. Ialdabaoth, according to France, is God's secret name. It means the child who wanders.

The child who wanders is Vera Cartwheel. This is not a casual correspondence. Vera's entire journey in the novel, from the loss of Miss MacIntosh in Chapter 13 through the long bus ride that frames the narrative and the accumulated weight of memory and hallucination and grief that constitutes her consciousness, is a wandering. She is not going somewhere. She is moving through the only territory available to her: the interior, where the authorities that once organized the world have collapsed and no replacement authority has arrived. The Ialdabaoth principle, that the problem is not the wrong authority but the assumption that authority resolves anything at all, is Young's deepest philosophical commitment. Vera does not find a new Miss MacIntosh. She finds that the wandering is the life, and that the child who wanders is not lost but is rather the only kind of self that is being honest about what selfhood actually is.

What France gave Young, understood as a structural principle rather than a set of doctrines, is this: the philosophical work happens in the space between the garden and the ladder. Not in the resolution of the tension between Epicurus and Plato but in the sustained inhabitation of it. The novel that takes this seriously cannot end with a position. It can only end when the conversation has been fully conducted. France's novels are long because the conversation is long. Young's novel is longer because she understood that the stream of consciousness is the only medium adequate to the full duration of that conversation. And the child at the center of that stream is Ialdabaoth: the wanderer, the one who cannot be returned to the cave once she has seen what the cave contains.

II. The Stream: William James and the Scale of Consciousness

Young stated directly, in interviews, that she admired and was influenced by both Henry and William James. William James's Principles of Psychology, published in 1890, is the book that gave the phrase stream of consciousness to literature and philosophy. It runs to 1,200 pages. The novel it inspired runs to 1,198.

This is not a coincidence Young would have been unaware of. She was a scholar as well as a novelist. She worked on Miss MacIntosh for eighteen years. The page count of a book one works on for eighteen years is not an accident; it is a decision, made over time, that the work was done when it reached its length and not before. A two-page difference from James's foundational work is the kind of precision that announces itself to anyone paying attention, which is precisely the kind of reader Young was building toward.

James's argument in the Principles can be summarized in four propositions: every state of consciousness is personal; states of consciousness are always changing; consciousness is sensibly continuous; and within consciousness there is a shifting and focused attention. The novel Miss MacIntosh is the proof of all four simultaneously, conducted at the scale that proof requires. You cannot demonstrate the continuity and the changefulness of consciousness in a short book. The demonstration requires the duration. The 1,200 pages are not excess; they are the minimum space in which the argument can be made honestly.

But James gave Young more than scale. He gave her permission to take seriously what the scientific and rationalist traditions had decided to exclude. In Is Life Worth Living?, James makes the point that much of human mental activity is forever closed to other minds in the way that the meaning of a surgical procedure is closed to the dog on the operating table. This is not a counsel of despair for James. It is liberating: it means that the things we cannot prove are not therefore absent, and that the irreducible interior life is not a failure of rigor but a feature of what consciousness actually is. Young's characters, especially Mr. Spitzer, inhabit this insight as their permanent condition. They know they cannot fully know. They continue anyway.

James also described what he called the stream's fringes: the felt sense of relations, the halo of half-formed meaning that surrounds every clear thought, the transitional states that connect one moment of consciousness to the next. These fringes are what most narrative fiction omits because they are difficult to render and seem to impede the plot. Young renders nothing else. The fringes are the novel. They are where the philosophical work is done: in the almost-thought, the remembered-and-not-quite, the grief that is not grief yet but has already begun.

III. The Blind God: Plato's Eros and the Novel's Two Poles

The Symposium is Plato's most dramatic philosophical work and his most direct treatment of Eros. It is, structurally, a contest of speeches: multiple voices, multiple frameworks for understanding love, none of them finally authoritative. Socrates arrives late, having become lost in thought on the way. Alcibiades arrives drunk and crashes the proceedings. The party ends in disorder with people falling asleep mid-conversation, and Socrates rises in the morning and walks to the Lyceum as though nothing unusual had occurred. The form of the Symposium enacts its argument: no single speech on Eros is sufficient, the truth is approached through the accumulation of competing accounts, and the one who knows most is the one who can hold the most perspectives simultaneously without demanding that they resolve.

This is the formal model for Miss MacIntosh, My Darling. The novel is a symposium at 1,198-page scale. Each major character holds a position on love, on reality, on death, on the self. None of them wins. The structure is the argument.

The specific Platonic concept that surfaces in the novel is Diotima's Ladder, also called the Ladder of Eros: the ascent from love of a particular beautiful body, through love of all beautiful bodies, through love of beautiful souls, through love of beautiful institutions and knowledge, to the final rung, the Form of Beauty itself, beauty as it purely is rather than as it appears in any particular instance. Diotima teaches Socrates that Eros is not a god but a daemon, a spirit intermediate between the human and the divine, born of Plenty and Poverty at Aphrodite's birthday banquet. Eros inherits from his father the pursuit of beauty and from his mother the fact of never having enough. He is perpetually reaching and perpetually lacking what he reaches for. That is his nature. That is love's nature.

Mr. Spitzer, the novel's central consciousness in its second half, is the character who carries this. He is an old lawyer who has never married, never reached his love, never arrived at the rung of the ladder where beauty is finally known. He dreams instead of the blind Eros: Young's exact phrase, in the novel, is that -

yet he dreamed of that blind Eros for whom there was no time and no face of love and no act of superficial recognition of subject or object and no love in this flesh and in this body but the love exceeding the limitations of the individual and of life and death

The blindness is not incidental. The traditional image of Eros is blindfolded, shooting arrows at random. But Young's blind Eros is something else: a love that has moved past the individual body, past the individual face, past the recognition of subject and object, into something that exceeds the limitations of individual life and death entirely. This is Diotima's highest rung, the Form of Beauty itself, but filtered through France's irony: Mr. Spitzer dreams of it. He does not reach it. The dream is real and the ladder is real and the arrival is not.

This is not tragic in the conventional sense. It is Young's philosophical position about what love actually is: the perpetual motion of reaching, not the attainment. And this maps directly onto Epicurus's counterpoint. The Epicurean maxim that death is nothing to us, that what is good is easy to get and what is terrible is easy to endure, that consciousness simply ceases and therefore the fear of death is irrational: this is the philosophy of the body, of the present moment, of the physical world taken seriously on its own terms. Young did not accept it as sufficient. But she did not discard it. She put it in the same novel as the blind Eros and let them address each other for 1,198 pages.

IV. The Pivot: Chapter Thirteen and the Garden of the Deaf

The moment in the novel where the France-Epicurus-Plato structure becomes most explicitly traceable is Chapter 13, the chapter Young designated the Garden of the Deaf. This is the pivot of the entire novel: the chapter in which Vera Cartwheel loses Miss MacIntosh, discovers her secret, and is assaulted; the chapter in which the stable world Vera had organized around Miss MacIntosh as anchor of the real is destroyed. After Chapter 13, Vera enters the novel's long second movement, the search for what was lost.

Chapter 13 opens with the farewell to Miss MacIntosh and passes immediately into the surreal, neglected garden where the ear is dead, sound is absent, communication has failed. Vera wanders through ghostly images: statues, flowers that fly away when touched, chessmen moving invisibly, the presence of historical figures from the history of medicine. The garden is not just a setting. It is the philosophical condition: the world after the loss of the organizing principle that made reality legible.

Young placed Anatole France, The Garden of Epicurus, and Heraclitus together in this chapter. She placed a direct link to a Heraclitian-Epicurean comparison. This is not background. It is the philosophical frame she built into the chapter's foundation. The garden of the deaf is the Epicurean garden stripped of its consolation: not the garden of pleasure and tranquility but the garden after the ear is dead, where even the Epicurean promise that what is terrible is easy to endure has broken down because the person carrying the burden is fourteen years old and has just lost the only thing she trusted.

And beneath it, Heraclitus: the river that is never the same twice, the war that is the father of all things, the opposites in perpetual conflict that produce the only harmony available. Young did not choose Epicurus in isolation. She chose the conversation between Heraclitus and Epicurus, the philosopher who said everything flows and the philosopher who said the flow is all there is and therefore there is nothing to fear. France staged that conversation in his garden. Young staged it again, at greater length, with a fourteen-year-old girl as the witness.

V. The Structure: Miss MacIntosh as Symposium

The argument of the previous four sections can now be stated as a unified claim about the novel's architecture.

Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is constructed on the model of Plato's Symposium as filtered through the ironic method of Anatole France and scaled to the 1,200 pages of William James's Principles of Psychology. The novel is a symposium: a sustained multi-voice contest of positions on love, reality, consciousness, and death, in which no single voice prevails and the form of the contest is itself the philosophical argument. The Symposium's structural principle, that the truth about Eros is approached through the accumulation of competing accounts rather than the declaration of a single correct position, is the structural principle of Miss MacIntosh at every level from the sentence to the whole.

The novel's two philosophical poles are Epicurus and Plato. Vera inhabits the Epicurean pole: the body, the present moment, the physical world taken seriously, the garden where pleasure and grief are both immediate and both real. Mr. Spitzer inhabits the Platonic pole: the blind Eros, the love that exceeds the individual, the perpetual reaching toward a form of beauty that is never arrived at, the ladder whose highest rung is always one rung higher than where he stands. Neither pole cancels the other. The novel holds them both for 1,198 pages.

France gives the method. He showed Young that the philosophical novel does not argue toward a conclusion. It stages a conversation that has been going on since Heraclitus and Epicurus looked at the same river and drew different conclusions. The conversation is still going. The novel is not an intervention in the conversation. It is the conversation, conducted at the full scale that James demonstrated consciousness requires. James gives the scale. The 1,198 pages are not excess. They are the minimum space in which the stream of consciousness can demonstrate, rather than merely describe, its four essential properties: that it is always personal, always changing, sensibly continuous, and marked by shifting and focused attention. The two-page difference from James's 1,200 is a signature, placed at the level of the whole, for readers who know what they are looking at.

Plato gives the animating question. What is the soul reaching toward when it reaches? Diotima's answer is the Form of Beauty, apprehensible finally only through reason, after the long ascent from body to soul to knowledge to the thing itself. Young's answer is the blind Eros: the dream of a love that exceeds the limitations of the individual and of life and death, held by a man who never arrives, who has spent his entire long life in the approach, and who dreams rather than attains. This is not a failure of the Platonic ladder. It is France's ironic translation of it: the ladder is real, the reaching is real, the highest rung is what the reaching is for, and the reaching is the life.

VI. The Shadow Count and the Symposium Structure

Two numerical facts about the novel support this reading and merit their own brief treatment.

The word shadow appears over 800 times in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling. Every character in the book is described as having a shadow except Miss MacIntosh and Vera. Miss MacIntosh, who commits suicide by walking into the ocean, cannot cast a shadow once Vera has seen her truly: the revelation destroys the stable surface that a shadow requires. Vera loses her shadow at the same moment she loses Miss MacIntosh, in Chapter 13, in the Garden of the Deaf.

This is Plato's Allegory of the Cave made literal and distributed across 1,198 pages. In the Cave, shadows are all the prisoners can know about the world. The philosopher who escapes the cave and sees the sun directly cannot return to the world of shadows without confusion. Vera's loss of Miss MacIntosh is her forced exit from the cave: she sees Miss MacIntosh as she actually is rather than as the shadow she had been content to accept. The seeing does not liberate her. It destroys the organizing structure of her world. This is Young's revision of Plato: the philosopher who escapes the cave does not arrive at wisdom. She arrives at the garden where the ear is dead. The ascent is real but the landing is not what was promised.

The question mark appears almost 4,000 times in the novel. Young built the entire novel around the Socratic method of relentless questioning. This is the Symposium's formal principle applied at the sentence level: the question is the unit of philosophical inquiry, not the assertion. The novel that questions 4,000 times is not a novel without answers. It is a novel that understands that the answer to a question about consciousness, love, death, and the self is another question, and that the stream of consciousness is the medium in which those questions are continuously posed and never finally resolved, because resolution would require the stream to stop, and streams do not stop.

VII. What This Means for Reading the Novel

Knowing this structure does not make the novel easier to read. Nothing makes Miss MacIntosh, My Darling easy. But it changes what you are looking for and what you are experiencing when you find it.

When Mr. Spitzer thinks of the blind Eros, you are not reading an obscure Platonic allusion buried in a difficult novel. You are at the novel's Platonic pole, the point furthest from the Epicurean garden, the point where the reaching has become so refined and so persistent that the specific face and body of love have dissolved and what remains is the pure motion of desire toward something beyond individual life and death. This is Diotima's highest rung. Mr. Spitzer never arrives there. He dreams of it. The dream is real.

When Vera wanders the Garden of the Deaf in Chapter 13 and Anatole France, Epicurus, and Heraclitus are beside her in that garden, the reader is at the novel's Epicurean pole, the point where the body's grief is immediate and unmediated and the philosophical consolations have not yet arrived, may not arrive, may be irrelevant to a fourteen-year-old whose world has just ended. France is there not as an authority but as a model: this is what it looks like when the conversation between materialism and transcendence is staged honestly, without premature resolution, in a garden where the ear is dead.

And the 1,198 pages are the James-scale in which the stream of consciousness, which is personal and changing and continuous and attentive and full of fringes and half-thoughts and griefs that are not yet grief, is given the room it requires to be honest about what it is. Young did not write a 1,198-page novel because she had too much to say. She wrote it because anything shorter would have been a lie about consciousness.

The novel is a symposium. France taught her the method. James taught her the scale. Plato taught her the question. She spent eighteen years answering it without ever answering it, which is exactly what the question requires.
