Miss MacIntosh, My Darling

The Philosopher of the Will

Arthur Schopenhauer's central claim is that the world we perceive, the world of objects and individuals and events, is a representation: a surface, an appearance, the veil of Maya. Behind it and beneath it and constituting it is the Will, a single blind irrational force that drives all existence without purpose or destination. The Will is not conscious. It does not desire any particular thing. It simply strives, endlessly, and every act of striving produces suffering because striving is by definition the experience of a lack that cannot be permanently filled. The individual self is the principle of individuation: the illusion that you are a separate entity with a separate fate. You are not. You are a temporary form through which the Will expresses itself before dissolving back into the underlying unity from which you were never really separate.

The ethical consequence is compassion. If the other's suffering is the same as your own because the underlying will is one, then the recognition of another person's pain as your pain is not sentiment but metaphysical accuracy. The artist's consequence is music: Schopenhauer placed music at the apex of the arts because unlike painting or poetry, which represent ideas or copies of the world, music bypasses representation entirely and speaks directly from the Will itself. It is not about the world. It is the world's innermost nature made audible.

Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is not a philosophical novel in the sense of dramatizing arguments. But Arthur Schopenhauer's philosophy is woven into the fabric of Mr. Spitzer so completely that it functions less as a reference and more as a diagnosis: the novel is describing what it actually looks like to live inside Schopenhauer's world, inside the Will and its suffering, inside the partial penetration of the veil, inside the impossible position of a man who has glimpsed the unity beneath individuation and cannot unsee it.

The Will-to-Live Kills Itself

Schopenhauer's most counterintuitive claim about suicide is that it is not the denial of the will-to-live but its most extreme expression. The person who kills themselves does so because the will-to-live has found its current circumstances intolerable. They are not negating the will; they are acting from it, trying to escape its suffering by destroying its vessel while leaving the underlying drive intact. Suicide affirms the will because it is the will refusing to accept its conditions. It is not liberation. It is the will in its most desperate form.

The novel dramatizes this argument through Peron. Mr. Spitzer works through the logic: "For what was fear, he had often asked himself, but the will to immortality, the aversion to death, either as the idea of an overwhelming fate or the extinction of the individual, and might not a man kill himself simply because of his overwhelming fear of death, his will to live, to live forever, and might he not seek that death which he had feared and embrace her as his love in an everlasting love... Suicide might be, far from the negative impulse it seemed, the most creative act, even like sexual love begetting another person, for suicide might be the desire to live, to live beyond the grave, beyond the limits of this life, to seek that consuming love which he had feared, so Peron had died, had died early."

This is not Mr. Spitzer rationalizing his grief. It is the novel engaging Schopenhauer's argument directly and extending it: what if suicide is not just an expression of the will but its most creative expression, the will's attempt to be born again into a form where it can finally get what it wants? Peron leaps from the tallest building in a cloud as a star flashed. He does not deny the will. He is the will at its most extravagant, most fearful, most reaching. Joachim stays. He is the will denying itself: the hesitant suicide who takes his luxurious time, the musician who writes only silent music, the man who lives on only to prolong the agony or in memory of his dead brother. The twins are not opposites in temperament. They are the will's two modes: the explosive affirmation that destroys its vessel, and the slow negation that outlives everything it loved.

Music as the Will Made Audible

Schopenhauer argued that music does not represent the Will's objects, its desires and their satisfactions. Music directly embodies the Will: the rising melody is striving, the resolution is momentary satisfaction, the dissonance is unsatisfied longing, the minor key is grief without consolation. Hearing music, we hear the Will itself, stripped of its representations, speaking in its own language. This is why music can move us to emotions we cannot name: we are hearing something prior to emotion, the drive from which all emotion comes.

The novel names Mr. Spitzer's music explicitly in Schopenhauerian terms: the music of the spheres, filling all space with its sound as of the human will, music his dead brother heard but which Mr. Spitzer could not hear, could only imagine in this silence. The music as of the human will: Young places the attribution directly. The music that Mr. Spitzer writes but cannot perform, the silent music that no living ear can hear, is music in Schopenhauer's sense: it is the will's direct expression, which is why it cannot be played on any instrument. Instruments play music about the will. Mr. Spitzer's music is the will itself, which has no instrument adequate to it.

The division between the brothers is the division between the will heard directly (Peron) and the will imagined in silence (Joachim). Peron heard the music of the will as of course he did, he who was the will's most extravagant expression, who lit fires wherever he went so he might follow himself. Joachim can only imagine it. He lives in the silence where the music should be, writing it down in notation that no orchestra can play, listening for it in the space between sounds, in the dying tide, in the lost musician with the withered string and the unuttered word. He is the man positioned one step outside the Will's direct language, the man for whom the world's innermost nature is permanently just beyond hearing.

Compassion Without Limit, Compassion With Limit

Schopenhauer's ethics rests on compassion as the recognition that the other's suffering is the same as your own, because beneath the illusion of separate selfhood, the will that suffers in them is the same will that suffers in you. The person who has partially seen through the principle of individuation, who has glimpsed the unity beneath individuation, feels the other's pain directly, without mediation, not because they are sentimental but because they are accurate.

Mr. Spitzer is described as sheltering by his compassion all the poor creatures incomplete and helpless and unknown: the derelicts, the hobo camp inhabitants, the Lady Macbeth actress drifting through the camps, the banker who does not know he is a banker, the cancer specialist who has crawled away to hide among the faceless ones. His compassion is not charity. It is the recognition that they are him, that he is them, that the differences of identity and history and social standing are the veil and the suffering beneath is one. He pays his dead brother's debts. He attends the opium lady for years without requiring anything from her. He cannot stop. Compassion of this kind is not chosen; it is the consequence of having seen, however briefly and incompletely, that the boundary between self and other is an illusion.

The novel also shows compassion with its limit, which is the point at which the veil reasserts itself. Mr. Bonebreaker has accepted Miss MacIntosh with her barren breast, her barren heart. The novel notes his compassion that had accepted her with these absences. But when she reveals her bald head he runs, slamming the door, causing the entire building to shake. His compassion had a bottom, an edge, a point at which the particular body before him reasserted its particular strangeness and he could no longer hold the unity. This is Schopenhauer's description of partial ethical development: the compassion that extends some distance through the veil and then, at some threshold of the strange or the unexpected, snaps back into the principle of individuation. He had counted on that compassion which had already accepted her barren breast, her barren heart. The acceptance was real. The limit was also real. He ran.

Individuation as Illusion: The Characters Who Blur

Schopenhauer argued that the sense of being a separate individual, distinct from all other individuals, is the fundamental illusion. It is not that you are wrong about most things and right about your own existence. The principle of individuation is itself the veil: you are not a separate entity with a separate will. You are the Will temporarily expressing itself through a particular form that will dissolve. Death is not the end of the Will; it is the end of one of the Will's temporary individuations. The Will continues in everything else that was ever alive and ever will be.

The novel's characters consistently blur into each other in exactly the pattern Schopenhauer describes. Mr. Spitzer wonders whether he and his brother were one and the same, though recognizing that this might be his own extinction. The heart specialist, testing in a midnight street, fears he might find the beatings of two hearts inside one body. The characters Jock, the Black Coachman, Joachim, and Peron may all be the same person: different individuations of the same underlying figure, the will expressing itself through multiple temporary forms that happen to coincide in one man's history.

Mr. Spitzer often wonders about his identity being confused with his dead brother's and this is applied to a man who was too literalist to be confused about his own identity, cuts through the literal reading. Mr. Spitzer is literally not confused. But the novel is telling us something the literal man cannot tell himself: he has become his brother because he was always his brother, because the principle of individuation that separated them was always an illusion, because the two hearts the physician would have found beating inside him are the same heart heard from two sides of the veil.

All who had taken their last shot were all the same. The billiard hall characters, the gamblers, the men who have reached the end of their particular individuation: at the level of the Will they are all the same, all expressions of the same striving that differs only in its temporary form. There was a place where all worlds, the highest and the lowest and the middle, should certainly be one, and no one should certainly be able to tell them apart. This is the place behind the veil of Maya. Mr. Spitzer has been glimpsing it all his life and cannot quite arrive there and cannot quite leave it behind.

The Opium Lady's Failed Renunciation

Schopenhauer admired the saints and ascetics who achieved genuine denial of the will: who withdrew from desire, who renounced the pleasures the will craves, who reached a state analogous to Buddhist nirvana through the systematic negation of the will's demands. This is the path he thought most worthy, not because it produces happiness but because it is the only honest response to a world that is constitutively suffering.

The opium lady looks like a Schopenhauerian denial of the will. She has withdrawn from the world. She lies in her bed behind drawn curtains. She has refused ordinary life, marriage, social engagement, and the demands of the present. She has gone by all other roads rather than the direct renunciation of life, preferring never the immediate moment of realization but an unearthly romance which should suffer no deterioration or change. She has renounced the world of ordinary time and its losses.

But the novel then shows that this is not the denial of the will. It is the will wearing the costume of renunciation. "Surely, my mother had evaded, wherever possible, the direct renunciation of life—going by all other roads—and had preferred never the immediate moment of realization but an unearthly romance which should suffer no deterioration or change brought by harsh experience inasmuch as it was not subjected to these mortal laws of change and chance and these accidents like the great snow avalanches falling over the leaden roofs with the sound of church bells tolling for the lost crystal-hunter, and surely she had loved that love which never was, yet was more powerful than any love which should be realized in this mortal sphere, the heavenly bridegroom none should see, the lover never to be discovered on this clouded earth—never, unless he should come in death’s guise, carrying her away." The love for the dead husband is the will-to-live at maximum intensity directed toward an object that cannot provide resistance. The will needs resistance; it strives against something. Her ghost-husband provides no resistance, no deterioration, no change, no disappointment. She can want him forever without the wanting ever being satisfied or frustrated in the ordinary sense.

She had evaded, wherever possible, the direct renunciation of life. The key word is evaded. Schopenhauer's renunciation is direct: you confront the will and say no to it. The opium lady's apparent renunciation is indirect: she says no to the world by saying yes, endlessly and without limit, to something the world cannot provide. This is not the saint's path. This is the will finding the one strategy that allows it to strive infinitely without exhausting itself. The drugs sustain the dreaming that sustains the love that sustains the will that keeps her breathing for the decades of the novel.

Two Watches: One for the Living, One for the Dead

Mr. Spitzer wears "two wrist watches, one which he wore on his right wrist, one which he wore on his left wrist which had no perceptible pulse beats, less than the quiverings of a dead moth or sparrow, his dead side, one which kept no time and was for the living so that he would miss his appointments, one which kept time and was for the dead so that he would not miss his appointments."

This is the AND Philosophy's grief as permanent weather pillar in its most Schopenhauerian form: the watch that keeps accurate time is the watch for the dead, the watch for Peron, the watch that was Peron's. The will-to-live expressed itself through Peron in time: he kept appointments, he raced, he gambled, he left fires so he could follow himself. The watch keeps time for him still, ticking on Mr. Spitzer's dead wrist, keeping the time of the will's most vital expression on the arm of the will's most subdued one.

The watch for the living keeps no time and is therefore useless for living. Mr. Spitzer misses his appointments. He walks the streets as if on thinnest ice, not knowing what hour it is, arriving too late or too early or at the wrong address. The world of the living, the world of the principle of individuation with its schedules and appointments and social engagements, is the world he has been losing his grip on since Peron died. The world of the dead, the world beneath the veil, the world where the will is one and all hearts beat together: that world he keeps perfect time for.

The AND Philosophy Reading

Schopenhauer's philosophy ends in the denial of the will: the sage who negates the will's demands, achieves equanimity, sees through the veil. The AND Philosophy does not end in denial of the will. It ends in the continued movement of the one who remains, still pulled by grief, still extending compassion, still wearing the dead brother's watch on the dead wrist, still hearing the music as of the human will in the silence where no instrument can play it.

The difference is this: Schopenhauer treats the denial of the will as an achievement, a state one can reach by sufficient philosophical clarity and sufficient ascetic practice. Young's novel treats it as a permanent condition of incompletion. Mr. Spitzer has seen through the principle of individuation far enough to know that the boundary between himself and his brother is illusory, far enough to know that the derelicts in the hobo camps are him, far enough to feel their suffering as his own and to extend his compassion without limit. But he has not reached the saint's total negation. He still wants Peron back. He still asks whether eternal recurrence might be the one law of life. He still wears both watches.

The AND Philosophy's plural self pillar is what Young takes from Schopenhauer: the self is not one, the boundary between selves is an illusion the will maintains for its own purposes, and the grief that crosses the boundary between the living and the dead is not pathology but accuracy. The grief as permanent weather pillar is what Young adds: the partial penetration of the veil is not a stage on the way to full enlightenment. It is the permanent condition. You see through the veil enough to suffer for everyone. You do not see through it enough to stop.

Don Quixote and the Windmill as Structural Motif in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling

Don Quixote's place among the six named quest traditions embedded in this novel. This chapter addresses something different: the windmill as a motif that Young distributed across 22 appearances in 12 chapters, assigned to every major consciousness in the novel, and used as a structural device that exceeds its source in Cervantes. All passages are drawn directly from the novel.

I. The Object in the Landscape

Chapter 6 contains the first physical windmill in the novel. It appears in the landscape through which the bus is traveling:

A derelict windmill stood in the midst of a flooded and vaporous field, its broken silver arm turning furiously in the wind.

This windmill is nobody's metaphor. It is an object in a flooded field, broken, turning furiously because the wind is turning it and not because any human intention has set it in motion. Its arm is broken. It is derelict. It turns anyway.

This is the windmill before it becomes anyone's symbol: a piece of machinery that has outlasted its purpose, still responding to external forces, unable to stop because stopping is not something windmills can choose. Young places this object in Chapter 6, after Moses has been called a mad Don Quixote chasing windmills in Chapter 1, and before the windmill becomes entangled with every other major consciousness in the novel. The derelict windmill in the flooded field is the motif's foundation: not a giant, not a delusion, not a metaphor yet. Just the thing itself, broken and still turning.

II. The Four Characters and What the Windmill Means to Each

The windmill attaches to four characters as an explicit descriptive or comparative device. In each case the attachment is made by a specific consciousness observing another character, or by the character observing themselves. The four attachments are not interchangeable. They say four different things about what a windmill is.

Moses Hunnecker: The Mad Don Quixote

The first explicit windmill attribution in the novel is Vera's assessment of Moses in Chapter 1:

Was he, after all, a bachelor, perhaps even some mad Don Quixote chasing windmills, a virgin spirit, nobody—and his family life, an emanation of my over-active imagination, really, my desire for established human relationships?

Vera is asking herself whether Moses is real. Whether his wife waiting at home is real. Whether the destination he is driving toward exists. The Don Quixote attribution is not an insult. It is a genuine question about the nature of the man at the wheel. Don Quixote's error was that he saw giants where there were windmills: he mistook the ordinary for the extraordinary, the mechanical for the monstrous. Vera is asking whether Moses has made the reverse error: whether he has mistaken the extraordinary for the ordinary, whether the life he believes he is driving toward is itself an illusion, whether he is going nowhere and calling it home.

Moses himself, later in Chapter 8, does not mention windmills. He talks about his hair, his politics, his quarrel with the doctor, Job's leviathan. The windmill attribution is Vera's reading of him, not his own self-image. This matters: Moses does not know he is Quixote. The observer applies the emblem. The character lives without it.

Cousin Hannah: The Human Windmill

Mr. Spitzer applies the windmill to Cousin Hannah twice in Chapter 52, and the application is intimate rather than dismissive. The first time:

Mr. Spitzer, turning the pages of old newspapers with almost faded print, had wondered what kind of a skirt this human windmill was searching for.

The second time, after her death:

She had been the human windmill, surely, turning even when the wind blew not—and in his absence had turned a page of the little book she had been reading when she died—had turned a page after she had died.

This is the most extraordinary windmill attribution in the novel. Cousin Hannah is the human windmill: she turns even when the wind blew not. She is not powered by external force the way the derelict windmill in Chapter 6 is. She generates her own motion. And she keeps turning after death: the page of the book she was reading turned after she died. The windmill does not stop when its operator dies. It has its own momentum.

Where Quixote saw a windmill as a giant, Mr. Spitzer sees Cousin Hannah as a windmill. He is not diminishing her. He is describing the nature of her energy: self-generating, continuous, not dependent on external conditions, still in motion after the body that housed it has stopped. The human windmill is the highest form of the motif in the novel. It is the windmill that has become autonomous.

Miss MacIntosh: The Windmill She Never Knew She Was

In Chapter 65, deep in the novel's second volume, another character says of Miss MacIntosh:

What had Miss MacIntosh been doing in Chicago? Chasing windmills. Miss MacIntosh had always been chasing windmills.

The windmill cards appear earlier, in Chapter 19, in Miss MacIntosh's own bedroom: almost translucent playing cards with curled edges and Dutch windmills on their silken backs. She plays with windmill cards and does not notice. She chases windmills and does not know it. The woman who embodied practical certainty, who trusted facts and geography and the clear reality of simple things, was all along a Quixote: she had a secret that contradicted her entire public performance, and the pursuit of the life she was performing, the sensible, the grounded, the undeceived, was itself the windmill she could never reach because she was not who she presented herself to be.

The windmill on the playing cards in Miss MacIntosh's bedroom sits on the backs of the cards: the side you do not see when you are playing the game. The windmill is on the hidden side of every card she holds.

Mrs. Hogden: The Woman Who Sold Her Windmill

Mrs. Hogden is the novel's fourth and most unexpected windmill figure. She does not chase windmills. She does not embody them. She lived in one. Her home on upper Long Island before she came to work for Catherine was an old Dutch windmill with winking eyes and broken arms. She sold it to take the job. Chapter 70 returns to this windmill seven times, more than any other single chapter in the novel, and the returns are increasingly elegiac.

The final windmill reference in Mrs. Hogden's arc is Mr. Spitzer's offer to restore her to her former position: "He called on Mrs. Hogden and, in the course of a long, somewhat painful interview, offered to restore her to her former position. She should have everything that she had lost, her Dutch windmill at a higher price than she had sold it for, a four-postered bed where she might sleep surrounded by effigies, everything, and enough money to last her the rest of her natural life and even perhaps a little longer. He was generous but not sure that Mrs. Hogden, smiling and beaming, had heard him rightly. She was so excited, he could not tell whether she was sad or happy. He believed that she was hardly sober."

While she lived in the windmill, an Arctic tern visited her every year. Young describes the tern as compelled by his own nature to circle the earth from pole to pole as if he were some kind of minor planet on its course in the starry endless heavens. The Arctic tern is one of the great natural questers: it makes the longest migration of any animal on earth, from Arctic to Antarctic and back, every year, without stopping. It visited Mrs. Hogden in her windmill annually for years and she found it distressing. She could not understand why it singled her out.

The windmill inhabitant received the world's greatest quester every year at her door and sold her home to go work in an opium house. The relationship between the windmill and the quest is most compressed here: the person who could have stayed in the windmill left it, and the quester who found the windmill every year kept circling.

The distribution is not random. The windmill is absent from the novel's opening bus chapters after Chapter 6, absent from the chapters in which Vera is most directly addressing her own consciousness, and concentrated in the Mr. Spitzer chapters of the second half, where it appears five times across Chapters 47 through 61. Mr. Spitzer is the character who sees windmills everywhere in the novel's second movement: in seagull wings, in rain drops, in book pages, in the woman he watched over for decades.

The windmill appears once in Catherine's vision in Chapter 37: there would be suddenly a whirling windmill. It materializes without explanation in her opium bedroom and disappears just as quickly. Catherine is the one character for whom the windmill is purely visionary: it is not applied to her as a description, and she does not live in one. It simply appears in her room.

IV. What Cervantes Built and What Young Did With It

Don Quixote's windmill scene is one of the most famous moments in Western literature precisely because it encodes a permanent question: who is deluded, the man who sees giants or the man who sees only windmills? Sancho Panza sees windmills. Quixote sees giants. The reader is invited to decide which perception is the error. Most readers decide Quixote is wrong. Cervantes arranged the scene so that certainty is harder to sustain than it appears.

Young took this question and distributed it across an entire novel. Every character in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is making the same determination Quixote made: is this thing in front of me what it appears to be, or is it something else? Miss MacIntosh insisted it was what it appeared to be and was wrong. Moses drove toward a home that may have been imaginary. Cousin Hannah fought for a cause with the energy of a windmill that turned without wind. Mrs. Hogden sold her windmill and went to serve an opium dreamer.

The windmill in Cervantes is a single object in a single scene. In Miss MacIntosh it is a thread woven through the entire novel from Chapter 1 to Chapter 70, touching every major consciousness, appearing in a flooded landscape as a physical object before it becomes anyone's metaphor, and finally resolving not into a symbol but into a home that could have been kept and was sold.

The derelict windmill in the flooded field of Chapter 6 is the novel's answer to both Quixote and Sancho. It is neither a giant nor merely a machine. It is a broken thing still turning. It has no operator and no purpose and it turns furiously anyway. That is not Quixote's delusion. That is not Sancho's practicality. That is what Young found when she looked at the windmill without either of them: a broken arm, a flooded field, and motion that has no reason to stop.

V. The Novel as Tissues, Not Issues

It could be that Miss MacIntosh, My Darling like Don Quixote is not a book of issues but of tissues: like an onion, layer after layer revealed on subsequent rereadings. The windmill distribution is the clearest demonstration of what this means at the level of a single motif.

On a first reading, the windmill in Chapter 1 is a passing metaphor for Moses's erratic driving and uncertain domestic claims. On a second reading it connects to Chapter 6's broken windmill in the landscape the bus is passing through. On a third reading it connects forward to Miss MacIntosh's playing cards in Chapter 19 and Cousin Hannah's posthumous page-turning in Chapter 52 and Mrs. Hogden's sold home in Chapter 70.

None of these connections are announced. Young does not say: remember the windmill from Chapter 1. She places the windmill and lets it accumulate. By the time Mr. Spitzer is walking through rain in Chapter 49 walking like a living windmill, the image has been alive in the novel for forty-eight chapters and has already been attached to Moses and will later be attached to Cousin Hannah and Miss MacIntosh and will appear seven times in Mrs. Hogden's story.

This is the tissue argument demonstrated: the windmill is a thread running through the novel's entire length, gathering meaning with each appearance, never announcing itself as a symbol, never asking the reader to stop and notice it. It turns continuously, like Cousin Hannah. It turns even when the wind blew not.

Search for him in dark valleys, search for him where Childe Roland had blown his horn

before a dark tower and where no other sound had ever been heard.

Miss MacIntosh, My Darling

The Poem and Its Ending

Robert Browning's 'Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came' (1855) is a poem about a knight who has been searching for the Dark Tower his entire life. He travels through a landscape of horror and failure: blighted plains, a starved horse, a river full of drowned men's hair, a field that seems designed to break the spirit of anyone who crosses it. Every knight who attempted this quest before him has failed. Their faces appear to him at the end like witnesses to his arrival. He reaches the tower. He sets his slug-horn to his lips. He blows. The poem ends.

He does not enter. He does not win or lose in any conventional sense. He arrives at the object of his entire quest and the poem stops at the moment of announcement: I am here. The ultimate fate is ambiguous. What matters architecturally is the formal structure: the quest that ends not in conquest or defeat but in the act of arriving and announcing oneself to something that will not answer. The horn blows. No other sound has ever been heard there. The tower does not open. The poem ends.

This is the formal model underlying the novel's treatment of its central impossible rescue: Cousin Hannah attempting to pull the opium lady out of her dark tower.

The Dark Tower in the Novel

The dark tower appears nine or more times in the novel, distributed across multiple characters and situations. It is never the same tower twice. It is always the same condition.

Vera lives in a dark tower. She dreams of a dark prince charming who should carry her away and rescue her from this dark tower. This is the fairy-tale register: the princess in the tower waiting for the rescuer. Miss MacIntosh knows nothing of this because it has never happened. The tower as imprisonment in fantasy, in the self's elaborate dreaming, guarded by a nursemaid who insists on the plain world outside. The opium lady lives in a dark tower. Her bedroom is the novel's most consistent dark tower: the high room in the sea-blackened house where Bengal lancers and sultans and long-dead poets come to visit, where she entertains a thousand visitors and cannot be reached by anyone who arrives in the flesh. Cousin Hannah wants to carry my mother away from this dark tower, to rescue her from opium dreams of the dead love. The tower here is not imprisonment by an external captor. It is a structure the opium lady has built and furnished and inhabited by choice. It is the most comfortable and well-populated tower in the novel. It is also completely inaccessible.

The husband is lost in a dark tower. The opium lady asks Cousin Hannah, when she travels through the Alps, to search for him in dark valleys, search for him where Childe Roland had blown his horn before a dark tower and where no other sound had ever been heard. The lost husband is Childe Roland: the knight who reached the tower and was never heard from again. The opium lady is waiting for him to return from the tower, not knowing whether he entered, whether he conquered, whether he blew his horn and was taken, whether he is still somewhere inside the walls.

The dead cry at dark towers. After the opium lady's death, her spirit still wanders, crying at many gates, knocking at many doors, arousing many watchmen in their dark towers, forever crying for the image of her love who had gone before her into the darkness. The tower multiplies in death: every gate is now a dark tower, every door a place where the dead cry and the watchmen do not answer.

Cousin Hannah as Childe Roland

Mr. Spitzer writes Cousin Hannah's epitaph in the novel's interior: here lies the greatest captain who fought against all nations and rescued many ladies from their dark towers and cruel lords but could not rescue herself. The formulation is exact. She rescued many ladies from their dark towers. Plural. She was a rescuer of prisoners from towers as her life's work. And she could not rescue herself, which means she too was in a dark tower of some kind, though the novel leaves the nature of hers implicit in the military language: she died in a domestic war, in her own old tent bed, with no aide-de-camp to see her go.

The journey to the opium lady's tower has the structure of Browning's poem throughout. Cousin Hannah travels through the failed landscape of the suffrage movement: the long winter marches, the desert treks, the battles against Turkish sultans and African kings, the journeys into forbidden Mecca. She passes, as Roland passes, through a territory littered with the evidence of previous failures: all the women who had tried to leave their marriages, all the ladies she had tried to carry away from monstrous loves and clouds and mirrors. She arrives at the opium lady's tower. She sets herself to the task. She blows her horn. No other sound has ever been heard there. The tower does not open. The poem ends.

Cousin Hannah is dead before the novel begins. She reached the tower. She announced herself. She is still announcing herself: her detonations of rage are still shaking the prisms in the house, the lace curtains are still billowing through the vast rooms with the memory of that wrath which would never spend itself. She blew her horn and the poem ended and the ringing is still in the walls.

The Tower That Cannot Be Entered

Browning's Dark Tower does not open when Roland blows his horn because the poem does not grant the tower an interior. The quest leads to arrival at an opaque exterior. What is inside the tower is outside the poem's knowledge. The tower's power is precisely its impermeability: it is the destination that can be reached but not entered, the object of the entire quest that refuses to resolve the quest by being openable.

The opium lady's tower is the same structure. It can be visited from outside: Mr. Spitzer comes every evening and sits in the great wing chair and whispers melodiously. Vera reads Pilgrim's Progress in both directions. The visitors come in their hundreds, the imaginary ones. But no one enters the tower's actual interior: the opium lady's inner life, the nature of her love for her dead husband, the content of the grief that has organized the house around her bed. These remain opaque throughout the novel. Vera witnesses from outside. Mr. Spitzer witnesses from outside. The reader witnesses from outside. The tower is described at immense length. It is never entered.

This is the AND Philosophy's witness pillar at its most structurally rigorous. The witness cannot enter the tower. The witness can only blow the horn: announce their presence, offer their attention, record what the exterior looks like. The opium lady is not withholding from the witnesses. She is simply in a place that cannot be entered from outside. The love that organized her life is not available for inspection. It is inside the tower. The tower is what it is. The horn rings against the walls and no other sound has ever been heard there and the poem ends and the ringing continues.

The AND Philosophy Reading

The dark tower thread is the AND Philosophy's illusion as primary pillar in its most concrete architectural form. The tower is where illusion lives: the opium dreams, the imaginary visitors, the dead husband who is always about to return from somewhere in the Alps. It is not a lesser reality than the world outside the tower. For the opium lady, it is the primary reality. The world outside the tower, the world Cousin Hannah is trying to pull her toward, is the secondary reality: the place where time passes and people age and the drugs run out and the clocks do not stop.

Childe Roland blows his horn at the boundary between the two realities. He has arrived from the outside world with all its blighted landscapes and failed knights. He has arrived at the place where the quest was always pointing. He announces himself at the threshold. The tower does not open because the threshold cannot be crossed. The two realities are not convertible. You cannot rescue someone from a primary reality by pulling them into a secondary one. You can only stand at the boundary and blow your horn and let the ringing carry through the walls and know that it is heard, even if no other sound comes back, even if the poem ends there, even if the ringing is still in the prisms decades later, still shaking the house.

Dante's Divine Comedy as Cosmological Map for Miss MacIntosh, My Darling

I. Mr. Spitzer's Belief

Mr. Spitzer believes that people need to travel through the lower world to reach the upper world. This is the summary of a passage in the novel that has not received the attention it deserves. It is a cosmological position stated explicitly by one of the novel's two primary consciousnesses. And the cosmological system it draws on is Dante's Divine Comedy: nine circles of Hell, seven levels of Purgatory, nine levels of Heaven, with God in the Empyrean beyond space and time.

Young cited Dante throughout Miss MacIntosh. Dante Alighieri is named directly in the novel. The Divine Comedy is referenced as a journey from sin to heaven, like Pilgrim's Progress. Roland appears in the Heaven of Mars. Boethius, whose De Musica the previous chapter addresses, is pointed out by Saint Thomas Aquinas in Dante's Paradiso. The Beatrice of Dante's Comedy, Beatrice Portinari who guides Dante through Paradise and symbolizes divine grace and theology, names a character in the novel's bus sections: Beatrice Fitzgerald, marginal, nearly blind, judged by her community, who may be royal by the bar sinister of her name. Dante's Cleopatra, whom he places in the circle of Lust, is echoed by the old woman in the novel who believes herself to be the reincarnation of Cleopatra.

These are not decorative allusions. Young embedded Dante's structure in the novel's movement. The question is where.

II. The Three Canticles and the Novel's Three Movements

The Divine Comedy has three books: Inferno, Purgatorio, Paradiso. Dante descends through Hell, ascends through Purgatory, and rises through Heaven. The journey is downward before it is upward, and the downward journey is necessary: without the full knowledge of Hell, the ascent through Purgatory and Paradise cannot be earned or understood.

Miss MacIntosh moves in a structure that rhymes with this even if it does not replicate it exactly. The novel opens with loss: Miss MacIntosh is gone. Catherine is in her opium bed. Vera is on a bus fleeing the house where she grew up. This is the beginning of the descent. The first half of the novel, roughly Chapters 1 through 43, moves through the lower world: the house by the sea, Catherine's dreams, Miss MacIntosh's secret revealed, Vera's loss of innocence in Chapter 13, Mr. Spitzer's early meditations on his dead twin brother and his unplayed music. These are the nine circles traversed slowly, the full accounting of what has been lost and what was never real.

The second half, roughly Chapters 44 through 82, moves through something that is not exactly Purgatorio but has its quality: the long process of each character arriving at what they actually are rather than what they have been pretending to be. Cousin Hannah's death and the revelation of her secret love. Mr. Spitzer's increasingly explicit meditations on the blind Eros and the love that exceeds the limitations of the individual. Esther Longtree's appearance as the mother of us all. These are not ascending toward Paradise. They are arriving at a kind of honest accounting. Dante's Purgatorio is the place where sin is acknowledged and purged. Young's second half is where illusion is finally named.

The Paradiso equivalent in Miss MacIntosh is not a location but a moment: the final chapter, Vera's declaration of love for the stone deaf man, her recognition of Esther Longtree as the mother of us all, the acceptance of her place in the wheel's rotation. It is not transcendence. It is acceptance. But acceptance, in this novel, is the highest rung available. The Empyrean is wherever Vera stops running and names what she loves.

III. The Seven Sins and the Seven Virtues

Dante's Purgatorio is organized around the seven deadly sins: Pride, Envy, Wrath, Sloth, Avarice, Gluttony, Lust. Each terrace of Purgatory is devoted to the purging of one sin. The corresponding virtues are taught on each terrace as the alternative to the sin being cleansed.

Every major character in Miss MacIntosh carries a dominant Dantean sin as their primary wound. Catherine's sin is closest to Sloth in its Dantean form: the failure to love adequately, the withdrawal from the demands of active engagement with the world, the opium bed as the physical expression of a soul that has abdicated its obligations. Miss MacIntosh's sin is Pride: the performance of a self she is not, the refusal to acknowledge the private reality that contradicts her public presentation. Mr. Spitzer's sin is Avarice in its emotional form: the hoarding of love never declared, the refusal to spend the self in relationship, the accumulation of grief and unexpressed devotion that never becomes actual giving. Vera's journey through the novel is the process of encountering these sins in the people who were supposed to teach her how to live, and arriving at something that is not virtue in the Dantean sense but is the honest acknowledgment of what each sin costs.

The seven levels of Purgatory with seven vices and seven virtues: this is the structural skeleton beneath Miss MacIntosh's second half. Young did not map the sins onto characters with academic schematicism. She absorbed the structure and built her own version of it, populated with characters whose wounds match the Dantean categories without reducing to them.

IV. Beatrice Fitzgerald and Beatrice Portinari

The novel's Beatrice is introduced on the bus, near the end of the bus journey section, as a figure of social marginality and judgment. She is nearly blind and losing the other eye. She is called a common prostitute by Madge, who resents her. She is called royal by Homer, who respects her name: Fitzgerald, with its prefix Fitz, meaning born of royalty on the wrong side of the blanket. She hides in darkness by putting out the lights so others will not see her. She has a son in the Navy who still remembers her.

Dante's Beatrice is the guide through Paradise, the figure who symbolizes divine grace and theology, the woman whose death in 1290 prompted La Vita Nuova and whose presence in the Comedy transforms the journey from a descent into Hell into a complete cosmological circuit. She appears at the top of Purgatory to relieve Virgil of his guiding function, which is reason's limit, and guide Dante through the levels of Heaven that reason alone cannot reach.

Young's Beatrice is not a guide. She is barely seen. She is almost blind. She hides. But the name carries its weight deliberately: royal by bar sinister, nearly sightless, marginal to the community that judges her, remembered by a son who has traveled the world. In a novel where Young said there are no coincidences, the name Beatrice attached to a woman who is going blind at the moment Vera's bus approaches the end of its journey is a structural marker. The guide through Paradise is losing her sight as the novel approaches its final reckoning. The Dantean figure who should be most visible is the one who puts out the lights so no one can see her. This is Young's revision of Dante: the divine mediator is not transcendent. She is exhausted and nearly blind and living in a tin house in a flooded yard.

V. What This Requires from the Novel

The Dante chapter is the architectural argument that most requires close verification against the novel's actual chapter structure. The three-canticle structure, the seven sins, the specific placement of Beatrice Fitzgerald as a Dantean revision: all of these need to be traced against the chapters as they exist, counting the specific positions and noting where the Dantean parallels hold and where Young departs from them.

What is established here is the framework and the evidence that makes the framework plausible: Young cited Dante directly and repeatedly; Mr. Spitzer explicitly articulates the lower world/upper world structure that is the Divine Comedy's organizing journey; the character named Beatrice carries the weight of her name in ways that are structurally coherent with the Dantean guide function; and the novel's movement from loss through reckoning to a final acceptance has the shape of the three canticles even if it does not replicate their theological content.

Dante's journey ends in the vision of God, a light that the soul finally apprehends after the full descent and ascent. Young's journey ends in Vera's love for the stone deaf man and her recognition of Esther Longtree as the mother of us all. The light that Vera finally apprehends is not divine but human: the love that persists through the impossibility of shared sound, the mother who carries all the stillborn children, the wheel that keeps turning after the hub is gone.

Mr. Spitzer was right. You have to go through the lower world first.

Reading Miss MacIntosh, My Darling for Its Structure

Marguerite Young was a student of Ronald S. Crane at the University of Chicago. Crane was a professor of aesthetics who believed in the novel as a poem, and he gave his students an assignment that Young described twice in separate interviews, years apart, with consistent precision. The class read Tom Jones thirteen times, doing an intricate study of its structure. Young's account of this discipline appears in the Roy Newquist interview and again in the Dalkey Archive interview with Miriam Fuchs and Ellen Friedman. The counts match. The novel is the same. The assessment is the same in both accounts.

From the Dalkey Archive interview:

We read Tom Jones thirteen times, doing an intricate study of its structure. Nothing could have been more valuable for my own writing, although it was one time more than I cared to read Tom Jones.

Marguerite Young, Dalkey Archive interview with Miriam Fuchs and Ellen G. Friedman

From the Roy Newquist interview:

We read Tom Jones thirteen times for its poetic structure. I have been grateful all my life for this beautiful discipline, for the adventure of spirit in regarding the novel as a poem and not merely a realistic or naturalistic document of some kind.

Marguerite Young, Conversations with American Writers, Roy Newquist

Tom Jones by Henry Fielding is the first great comic novel in the English language, organized around a structural principle that its surface actively conceals: everything that appears to be a digression is load-bearing, every subplot returns to the main plot, and the apparent disorder of the narrative conceals a meticulous architecture of cause and consequence beneath it. You cannot see this architecture on a first reading. You can barely see it on a third. Crane assigned thirteen readings because the structure of Tom Jones does not become fully visible until the reader has accumulated enough familiarity with every element to see how each element relates to every other.

Young absorbed this principle and spent eighteen years applying it to a novel that looks nothing like Tom Jones. Miss MacIntosh, My Darling has no ironic prefatory essays calling attention to its architecture. It does not announce its structure. It moves in spirals and returns and accumulations that feel, on a first reading, like digression. This is intentional. Young built a novel whose deep architecture is invisible until the reader has spent enough time inside it to begin to see how it is organized.

This series of chapters is the record of one reader spending enough time inside it.

What Young Said About the Structure

Young described the novel's architecture directly in the Dalkey Archive interview. The description is the clearest statement of structural intent she ever made about Miss MacIntosh, My Darling:

She is the central character with all the spokes of other characters radiating out from her. I always thought of Miss MacIntosh as the center of the wheel, the hub, then the spokes as the subsidiary, secondary characters, and the wheel as endlessly expanding like a universe.

Marguerite Young, Dalkey Archive interview with Miriam Fuchs and Ellen G. Friedman

The wheel with Miss MacIntosh at the hub and the other characters as spokes is the architect's description of the blueprint. Young did not offer this as an interpretation of the novel. She offered it as a description of how she built it. The chapters that follow take this description as their starting point and ask what the wheel actually contains: what the spokes are made of, what the hub's absence means after Miss MacIntosh walks into the sea in the opening pages, and what holds the wheel together when the center is gone.

Young also described the novel's structural tradition. When asked in the Dalkey Archive interview whether she considered herself experimental, she said:

I see myself as traditional even though I know you see my work as experimental. I don't really consider Sterne, Joyce, and Proust experimental either because the tradition of their writing goes back a long way. Traditional. The Grand Tradition. Clear back to Don Quixote.

Marguerite Young, Dalkey Archive interview

And when asked why the novel has no beginning, middle, or end:

Because life has no beginning, middle or end.

Marguerite Young, Dalkey Archive interview

These statements together define the project these chapters undertake. The novel is traditional, not experimental: its roots run back through Sterne and Cervantes to the oldest narrative traditions in the language. It has no beginning, middle, or end because it was built on a structural principle, the wheel, the hub-and-spoke, that does not depend on linear progression. And it was built by a writer who had been trained to read a novel thirteen times before she trusted her understanding of how it was constructed.

What This Series Does

The Deep Architecture series examines the novel's structural foundations: the philosophical and literary traditions Young embedded in the novel's architecture, the formal devices she used at the sentence and chapter level, and the patterns that become visible only across the novel's full length.

The sections are organized by architectural layer rather than by chapter sequence. Each movement addresses one structural element: the wheel and its spokes, the Boethian musical system, the Dantean cosmological map, the bus as cosmic vehicle and the named passengers it carries, the quest traditions accumulated across four thousand years of literary history, the windmill as a motif threaded through the novel from Chapter 1 to Chapter 70, the question mark as a formal device distributed with structural intention, and the onomastic architecture of the names Young gave her characters.

None of these structural elements are announced in the novel. Young did not label her chapters with their Dantean canticle or their Boethian musical category. She placed the derelict windmill in a flooded field in Chapter 6 and did not return to it explicitly until Chapter 19, and did not name Miss MacIntosh a windmill chaser until Chapter 65. She gave the Egyptian sailor directions through the labyrinth in Chapter 2 and did not name the minotaur as something not to fear until midway through those directions. She put the question mark in the novel 3,998 times and distributed it in patterns that only become visible when counted.

This is what thirteen readings of Tom Jones taught her to do: to build a structure that the reader cannot see on the first encounter, that accumulates across the full length of the work, and that rewards the reader who stays long enough to feel its weight.

A Note on Evidence

Every architectural claim in this series is grounded in the novel. The series draws on Young's interviews and essays throughout, particularly the Dalkey Archive interview with Fuchs and Friedman, the Roy Newquist interview, the Charles Ruas interview, and the essays collected in Inviting the Muses. Young spoke precisely about her work when asked the right questions. The interviews are primary sources and are treated as such.

The series also draws on direct analysis of the novel, including counts of the question mark distribution across all 82 chapters, word-by-word searches for motifs and allusions, and close reading of passages whose structural significance became apparent only through the accumulation of related findings elsewhere in the novel.

This is, in other words, an attempt to read Miss MacIntosh, My Darling the way Ronald Crane read Tom Jones with his students at the University of Chicago. Not thirteen times. But enough times to begin to see what Young built.

Young's Own Final Word on How to Read It

In the last interview Miriam Fuchs conducted with Young before her death in 1995, Fuchs asked Young how she would advise people to read Miss MacIntosh, My Darling. Young said they should not take it so seriously. They should read it for the humor.

Then she said:

They can always read it again, if they like it. At different periods in your life you see a different book.

Marguerite Young, final interview with Miriam Fuchs, June 1993

The Deep Architecture series is one reader's account of what becomes visible after many readings, at one particular period of life, in one particular place. Other readers at other periods will see other books. Young expected this. She built the wheel so that each spoke could be entered from the rim, and the center would look different depending on where you stood.

The door is open. Come in.

Definition from research

Was it possible that she had always been this pale Don Juan beneath her mask, this gentleman so frail, changeable, uncertain, evasive that his might have been a lady's trembling heart and tendency to faint, fall, slip into a simulated unconsciousness where

all might be permitted which was never permitted by consciousness?

Miss MacIntosh, My Darling

The Legend and Its Stone Guest

Don Juan is one of the foundational figures of Western literature: the libertine, the seducer, the man who pursues every woman and commits to none, who kills the father of one of his conquests and then, when the dead man's statue comes to dinner and invites him to return the visit, laughs and goes. In the original telling and in Mozart's Don Giovanni, Don Juan meets the statue at the graveyard, takes its stone hand, and is dragged down to hell unrepentant. He could have repented. He refuses. The defining characteristic of Don Juan is not his seductiveness but his refusal of the final reckoning: he will not account for what he has done. He will not change. He is dragged down without yielding.

The Don Juan tradition has a stone guest: the murdered father returned as a monument, as weight, as the inescapable consequence of the seducer's actions made material and permanent. The stone guest comes to dinner. The stone guest invites him to supper in return. Don Juan goes. He is taken. The stone guest is what happens when you refuse accountability long enough: the consequence becomes architecture, becomes something that can grip your hand and pull.

Mr. Spitzer at the Deathbed

Mr. Spitzer is at the opium lady's deathbed. She is dying. She is in the final hours, babbling, revealing vanished life, speaking more often of the remote past than of the future. Mr. Spitzer is managing his own grief and tactfulness simultaneously: keeping her talking about cities buried under desert sand rather than tomorrow's weather, encouraging her to take another city by storm rather than contemplate the great abyss toward which she headed. He is doing what he always does: witnessing, accommodating, apologizing for his presence, making himself useful at the edge of something he cannot enter.

And in the middle of this, he wonders: was it possible that she had always been this pale Don Juan beneath her mask, this gentleman so frail, changeable, uncertain, evasive that his might have been a lady's trembling heart and tendency to faint, fall, slip into a simulated unconsciousness where all might be permitted which was never permitted by consciousness?

This is one of the novel's most architecturally compressed sentences. Mr. Spitzer is asking whether the opium lady, whom everyone in the novel has experienced as the one who was loved and pursued and courted and visited, was actually herself the seducer: the one who was always frail and changeable and evasive precisely because commitment was what she refused, who slipped into unconsciousness when reality pressed its claim, who permitted in dreams what she denied in waking life, who has been conducting, all this time, a Don Juan career from her bed.

The Female Don Juan

The gender inversion is everything. Don Juan is by definition masculine: his project is the conquest of women, his refusal of consequence is coded as male prerogative, his punishment is being dragged to hell by a dead man's stone hand. He moves through the world. He pursues. He refuses to be held.

The opium lady does not move. She has not left her bed in years. She does not pursue anyone; they come to her. She does not seduce in any conventional sense; she is visited, entertained, courted by an endless procession of the living and the dead. But Mr. Spitzer's question proposes that this is the more perfect form of the Don Juan strategy: not to pursue but to attract, not to move but to be the fixed point around which everyone orbits without ever reaching the center, to be so frail and changeable and evasive that no one can pin down what she wants, what she loves, what she would accept, whether she is present or absent, real or dreamed.

She has loved, by her own account, one man: her dead husband. But this love is organized entirely around his absence. He is dead. He cannot come back. The love that is organized around permanent absence is the perfect Don Juan love: it requires no commitment because the beloved cannot be present to demand it. She can love without limit because the limit has been set by death. She can be the pale Don Juan because her one true conquest is already a ghost, already a stone guest who cannot arrive for dinner, and she is therefore permanently safe from the reckoning that dragged the original Don Juan down.

The Stone Guest Who Never Came

In the Don Juan legend, the stone guest comes. The dead father, whose death was Don Juan's fault, returns as stone, comes to dinner, issues the invitation, arrives at the graveyard supper, takes the hand, drags him down. Don Juan is punished because the stone guest comes.

The opium lady's stone guest never comes. Her dead husband does not return as monument and consequence. He does not come to dinner. He is not a stone guest. He is a dream guest, a fog guest, an opium guest who arrives in the bedroom as a vision and does not grip any hand and drag anyone anywhere. The husband's love was dead, as Cousin Hannah told her: but she did not seem to know that death was necessary to her love. The death is what makes the love safe. The stone guest cannot drag you to hell if the stone guest never materializes. The opium lady has found the Don Juan strategy's one successful variant: love the dead man, who will never become a stone guest, who will never demand the reckoning, who will never grip the wrist. Mr. Spitzer at the deathbed is watching the pale Don Juan die without ever having been dragged to hell. This is not a triumph. It is not a failure either. It is what life looks like when it ends on its own account without anyone's permission or objection or desire, as Mr. Spitzer describes his own slow suicide. The stone guest did not come. The hell was not incurred. The woman who slipped into simulated unconsciousness where all might be permitted died in her bed, in her tower, with her imaginary visitors and her ghost husband and her faithful witness sitting in the wing chair beside her, and the stone hand never gripped her wrist, and she went down anyway, because everything goes down, with or without the stone guest, because the abyss is there whether Don Juan laughs at it or not.

The AND Philosophy Reading

The pale Don Juan identification is the AND Philosophy's plural self applied to the question of how desire organizes a life. The opium lady has been read throughout the novel as the passive figure: the one who lies in bed, the one who is loved and visited, the one who requires care and management. Mr. Spitzer's deathbed question proposes that this reading has the agency exactly backward. The frail, changeable, uncertain, evasive figure is not the passive recipient of the story. She is its engine. She has been running a Don Juan operation from her bed for decades: attracting rather than pursuing, being elusive rather than direct, permitting in dreams what consciousness refuses, organizing everyone else's life around the impossibility of reaching her.

The grief as permanent weather pillar: the love organized around permanent absence is not a failure of love. It is the most sustained and consistent love in the novel. She has loved her dead husband without interruption for the entire narrative. The love has not faded. It has not transferred. It has not compromised. It has simply required that its object be perpetually unavailable, which the dead are. This is the pale Don Juan's resolution of the Don Juan problem: the seducer who cannot commit finds the one beloved who cannot demand commitment, and loves them without limit, and slips into the unconsciousness where all is permitted, and the stone guest never comes, and the love continues, and she dies in it, still in it, the pale Don Juan whose hell never arrived, whose love was exactly as permanent and exactly as organized around absence as the grief of everyone who loved her.

Definition from research

Midway through Miss MacIntosh, My Darling, Mr. Spitzer contemplates what his dead brother Peron may have established by dying: "a colony under no flag, perhaps upon the other shore, a community not of this world as now it was but of this world as once it was...or of this world as it might become tomorrow." The passage is dense with grief and longing, and it would be easy to read it as only that: a mourning man's wish that death might lead somewhere better than here. But Young is doing something architecturally more precise. She is embedding a constitutional vision inside an elegy. The community not of this world as now it was but as it might become tomorrow is not a description of the afterlife. It is a description of a just world. And the novel has been building toward it for five hundred pages before it arrives.

The phrase "colony under no flag" is Young's most compressed statement of what the AND philosophy requires politically. A flag represents sovereignty, jurisdiction, the authority of one group to define who belongs and who does not, whose body is protected and whose is expendable, whose voice counts and whose is silence. Young had spent seven years at New Harmony, Indiana, the utopian community where Robert Owen and the Harmonists tried to build a society organized on principles of common ownership, universal education, and the rejection of hierarchy. Angel in the Forest, her book about those experiments, was published in 1945. She began Miss MacIntosh, My Darling two years later, carrying everything she had learned about why utopias fail and what they nonetheless prove. The colony under no flag is what remains when you strip away the specific failures and look at the aspiration that kept generating new attempts. It is the world as it might become tomorrow.

The five pillars of Young's philosophy all produce specific constitutional requirements when they are applied to the question of how a society should be organized. The plural self pillar insists that no person is reducible to a single identity, which means no constitutional provision that treats a person as only one thing, only a worker or only a citizen or only a body, can be adequate. Every heart is the other heart: the political consequence is that your suffering is my obligation, not because you are like me but because the boundary between us is an illusion the dominant culture uses to manage which grief it will acknowledge and which it will ignore. The economic floor pillar, which Young makes explicit in AND: the novel's argument that the five pillars require a material floor as their precondition, is already present in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling in the figure of every person who cannot access what their humanity requires. Mr. Spitzer practices law without fee, "preferring the lost causes." Esther Longtree moves slowly behind the counter with a deformed foot and no one who will bear the cost of her care. The bus driver Moses Hunnecker will retire into nothing. The novel is full of people for whom the economic floor does not hold, and the colony under no flag is the world in which it does.

The witness pillar's political consequence is the most direct: a community that cannot see its own dispossessed members cannot address their condition. The novel insists on visibility for everyone it contains: the bus passengers, the pregnant waitress, the deaf man, the stillborn children who embarrass Esther because she cannot explain them. Young gives each of them the full weight of sustained, undiscriminating attention that the witness pillar requires. The colony under no flag is the community that has learned to witness without hierarchy, in which no life is too ordinary to be seen.

The grief as permanent weather pillar's political consequence runs through the novel as the question of what happens when grief is collective. The mother Catherine's opium grief, Miss MacIntosh's grief over her mastectomy and her isolation, Mr. Spitzer's grief over his brother, Hannah's grief over the love that became the suffrage movement, Esther Longtree's grief over forty years of stillborn children: none of these are private sorrows. They are the weather of a society that has not built the structures its members need to survive. The colony under no flag is the world organized around the permanent weather rather than the fiction that grief is temporary and individual and properly kept indoors.

The most unexpected element of the colonial vision in the novel is what Young gives it as a foundation: the stone deaf man at the novel's end, whose deafness became complete when he was fourteen and who was consoled by an old Black woman who told him: "All must suffers for something that be not their fault, you because your skin be white and we because our skin be black." This speech, which arrives late in the novel and which Young gives in the woman's own voice without correction or translation, is the closest the novel comes to a direct constitutional statement. The colony under no flag is the community that takes this woman's understanding as its operating premise: that suffering distributed by circumstances of birth is not natural order but injustice, that the white boy and the Black woman share a condition even when their specific oppressions differ, and that the appropriate response is "dream on, for life is imaginary, and this be an imaginary world." The imagination is not escapism. It is the faculty by which the world as it might become tomorrow is held in view against the world as now it is.

Young was writing this in 1947. The Civil Rights Act was seventeen years away. The Voting Rights Act was eighteen years away. The AND Philosophy, in which you would formally develop the constitutional provisions that the five pillars require, was decades away. But the colony under no flag is already in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling, embedded in an elegy for a dead brother, spoken by a grieving man standing on a beach with music only he can hear, dreaming of a community that has not yet been built and may never be built and must nonetheless be imagined because the imagining is what keeps it possible. This is what Young's philosophy produces when it meets the question of how people should live together. Not a manifesto. Not a platform. A colony under no flag, upon the other shore, in the world as it might become tomorrow.

Young's Own Structural Metaphor and the Novel as Radial Architecture

I. Young Speaks

Marguerite Young described the structure of Miss MacIntosh, My Darling in her own words, in interviews, and the description is precise: the characters are the spokes of a wheel with Miss MacIntosh at the center. This is not a critic's retrospective metaphor. It is the architect describing the blueprint. And it is a description that, once heard, reorganizes everything about how the novel is read.

The wheel metaphor appears twice in the research assembled for this project, drawn from two separate interview sources. Its repetition confirms it was not a passing remark. Young returned to this image when asked to explain what she had built. The wheel was her word for it. The spoke was her word for each character. Miss MacIntosh, the practical governess from What Cheer, Iowa, who walks into the ocean in the first pages and is never seen again, is not a character among characters. She is the hub. She is the structural center around which every other life in the novel rotates.

What the wheel metaphor does that linear narrative metaphors cannot: it explains why the novel can be 1,198 pages long without feeling like it is going somewhere in the conventional sense. A spoke does not go anywhere. A spoke rotates. Each character in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is in motion relative to the center, but the motion is circular rather than progressive. The novel does not build toward a climax. It accumulates revolutions. Each chapter adds another arc of a character's orbit around the absent center.

II. Hegel and the Circle of Circles

Beside Young's wheel metaphor a second structural image sits: Hegel's philosophical concept of the circle of circles, noted in connection with the phrase things have worlds and worlds inside. This is not a casual juxtaposition. Young read seriously and placed her images with intention. The Hegelian circle of circles describes a philosophical system in which each concept is itself a whole, and the whole is a system of wholes, each internally complete and each in relation to all the others.

This maps onto the novel's structure with remarkable precision. Each character in Miss MacIntosh is a world complete in itself. Catherine Cartwheel's chapters are not interruptions of Vera's quest; they are their own cosmos, their own accumulation of grief and illusion and history. Mr. Spitzer's meditation on love and death and the silent music he composes for an audience of the dead is not subordinate to any other narrative thread; it is complete in itself. Esther Longtree's perpetual pregnancy and her stillborn children are not a subplot; they are a world, existing fully alongside every other world in the novel.

The wheel and the circle of circles are the same structure described at different scales. The wheel describes the spatial relationship of the characters to the absent center. The circle of circles describes the internal organization of each character's consciousness: each is itself a world, and the novel holds all of them simultaneously, in the same way that Hegel's system holds each concept simultaneously as part and as whole.

Young was not illustrating Hegel. She arrived at the same structural principle through her own eighteen years of building. But knowing that the principle has a name, and that the name comes from the same philosophical tradition she was drawing on for the Symposium and Boethius and James, confirms that what Young built was not intuitive but architecturally deliberate.

III. What the Hub's Absence Does

The most architecturally significant fact about the wheel metaphor is what it implies about Miss MacIntosh herself. If she is the hub, and she is absent from the novel almost immediately, having walked into the ocean before the first chapter ends, then the novel is a wheel rotating around an empty center. The spokes are in motion. The hub is gone.

This is not a flaw in the structure. It is the structure's central argument. Every character in the novel is organized by their relationship to something that is no longer there. Vera's quest is literally the search for Miss MacIntosh, for What Cheer, Iowa, for the stable reality that Miss MacIntosh represented. Catherine's opium dreams are the inverse: the construction of an alternative hub, an imaginary center that keeps the world from spinning into chaos without Miss MacIntosh to hold it. Mr. Spitzer's endless meditations on love and death are the orbits of a spoke that has lost its center and keeps moving anyway, composing music for no one, practicing law in courts that may not exist, faithful to the structural motion of his orbit even though what he orbits is gone.

The wheel with the missing hub is also Young's philosophical argument about the self. The plural self, which is the first pillar of the AND philosophy, cannot be unified around a single center because the center the self was organized around is always already lost. Miss MacIntosh is the wig. The wig comes off in Chapter 13. The spokes keep rotating because that is what spokes do: they rotate. What they rotate around after the hub is gone is the memory of the hub, the absence of the hub, the shape of the space where the hub was.

IV. Esther and Mr. Spitzer as Poles

Young told interviewers that Esther Longtree, who appears at the end of the novel, is the mother of us all. In the same interview she said Mr. Spitzer is the father of us all. This pairing, the mother and father of all the novel's characters, is the wheel's outermost poles: the two spokes that are furthest from each other while remaining attached to the same center.

Esther Longtree is perpetually pregnant, perpetually losing her children to stillbirth, perpetually carrying what cannot be born. Mr. Spitzer is perpetually composing music that cannot be heard, practicing law in courts that may not exist, faithful to a twin brother who is dead and to a love he never declared. Between them: all the other spokes, all the other characters, all the other orbits. The wheel turns. The hub is absent. The spokes keep their distance from each other and their attachment to the missing center.

The novel's last movement is Vera's arrival in Indiana, the heart of the Middle West, where she encounters Esther and the stone deaf man she falls in love with. The quest that began with the loss of Miss MacIntosh ends not with the recovery of the center but with Vera accepting her place as one of the spokes. She has found the mother of us all. She has completed her orbit. The wheel does not stop turning.

V. Reading with the Wheel in Mind

Knowing Young's wheel metaphor changes what a reader looks for and what a reader notices. The novel is not a linear narrative that has gone wrong by being too long and too circular. It is a radial structure that is exactly the right length for what it is: a system in which each spoke completes enough of its orbit to demonstrate that the orbit is real, and that the center it orbits is gone, and that the motion continues anyway.

The question the novel asks at the level of its whole structure is the same question it asks at the level of every character's interior: how does a consciousness organize itself when the organizing principle has been removed? The spokes answer: by continuing to rotate. By staying in motion relative to the empty center. By accumulating the memory of the hub in the very structure of the orbit.

That is the wheel. That is the novel. Young built it in eighteen years and described it in one word: spokes.
